title: Semi-analytic Inference of Satellite Densities in the Cold Dark Matter Model Part I. Comparison to Ultra-faint Dwarf Kinematics
comment: 22+11 pages, 8+6 figures, video abstract at https://youtu.be/dal8_lRz3EI
summary: Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies are critical testing grounds for probing the limits of galaxy formation in the cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm. Employing a semi-analytic cosmological satellite generator that captures the expected CDM halo population, we estimate Milky Way dwarf density profiles through two methods: a kinematic approach using stellar velocity dispersions and a separate method based on dwarf stellar masses. The kinematic approach yields a larger diversity in central dark matter densities than expected from the CDM population, as inferred from the stellar-to-halo mass relation, with compact ultra-faints appearing overdense and larger systems appearing underdense. For the ultra-faint dwarfs with at least 10 stars with spectroscopic measurements, this discrepancy persists at the ~2.4$σ$ level across all considered systematic variations on the semi-analytic modeling. Our framework introduces a novel, robust procedure for testing the consistency of the observed population of Milky Way satellites with cosmological expectations. As future surveys discover new dwarf satellites and refine stellar velocity measurements, updating this analysis will provide an increasingly stringent test of the CDM paradigm.

AI.tldr: The paper tests cold dark matter (CDM) predictions for Milky Way ultra-faint dwarf galaxies using a semi-analytic cosmological satellite generator. Two methods for estimating dwarf density profiles—one kinematic, one mass-based—reveal that kinematic estimates show greater diversity in central dark matter densities than expected from CDM, with a ~2.4σ discrepancy persisting across systematic variations for ultra-faints with ≥10 spectroscopic stars. This provides a novel robustness framework for testing CDM against future observations.
AI.motivation: Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies serve as critical probes for testing the limits of galaxy formation within the CDM paradigm, and the paper aims to examine whether observed central dark matter densities in these dwarfs are consistent with cosmological CDM expectations.
AI.method: A semi-analytic cosmological satellite generator capturing the expected CDM halo population is used to estimate Milky Way dwarf density profiles via two independent methods: (1) a kinematic approach using stellar velocity dispersions, and (2) a method based on dwarf stellar masses.
AI.result: The kinematic approach produces greater diversity in central dark matter densities than CDM predicts from the stellar-to-halo mass relation: compact ultra-faints appear overdense while larger systems appear underdense. For ultra-faint dwarfs with ≥10 spectroscopically measured stars, the discrepancy holds at ~2.4σ significance across all considered systematic variations in the semi-analytic modeling.
AI.conclusion: The framework introduces a robust, novel procedure for testing the consistency of observed Milky Way satellites with cosmological expectations. As future surveys discover new dwarf satellites and refine stellar velocity measurements, updating this analysis will yield increasingly stringent tests of the CDM paradigm.

title: Superdiffusion at the Galactic Centre
summary: Tracking S-star cluster orbits around Sgr A* calibrates orbital transport models for space-borne gravitational wave detectors. Standard kinetic theories model this cluster via local Fokker-Planck equations, which predict that general relativistic precession halts angular momentum diffusion at the Schwarzschild barrier. Because inverse-square gravitational encounters generate a Holtsmark torque distribution with infinite variance, resonant relaxation operates as a space-fractional process governed by non-local Lévy flights. We simulate this superdiffusive continuous-time random walk using a Markov chain initialized with empirical S-star orbits, including the recently observd S301. Integro-differential fractional operators allow trajectories to cross regions of quenched local diffusion without density buildup at the barrier. Non-equilibrium regimes yield immediate linear flux growth, while secular tidal heating at periastron inflates stellar radii to shift disruption boundaries. Regularized backward integration of the fractional transport equation traces current phase space configurations back to initial deposition states, matching the energy requirements of the \emph{Fermi} bubbles. Relativistic precession does not suppress mass-ratio inspiral rates, which provides a model for event topologies in target galactic nuclei.

AI.tldr: This paper models the S-star cluster around Sgr A* using a space-fractional Fokker-Planck approach, treating resonant relaxation as a superdiffusive Lévy flight process. Simulations with a Markov chain initialized from empirical S-star orbits (including S301) show that trajectories cross the Schwarzschild barrier without density buildup, produce linear flux growth in non-equilibrium regimes, and match Fermi bubble energy requirements via backward integration.
AI.motivation: Standard local Fokker-Planck kinetic theories predict that general relativistic precession halts angular momentum diffusion at the Schwarzschild barrier. However, since inverse-square gravitational encounters generate a Holtsmark torque distribution with infinite variance, resonant relaxation is fundamentally non-local (space-fractional). The authors aim to incorporate this superdiffusive behavior to better model S-star cluster dynamics and calibrate orbital transport models relevant to space-borne gravitational wave detectors.
AI.method: The authors simulate a superdiffusive continuous-time random walk (CTRW) as a Markov chain initialized with empirical S-star orbits including the recently observed S301. They employ integro-differential fractional operators that allow trajectories to cross regions of quenched local diffusion without density accumulation at the barrier. Non-equilibrium regimes and secular tidal heating at periastron are incorporated, along with regularized backward integration of the fractional transport equation to trace phase-space configurations back to initial deposition states.
AI.result: The fractional (non-local Lévy flight) formulation permits trajectories to cross the Schwarzschild barrier without density buildup. Non-equilibrium regimes yield immediate linear flux growth. Secular tidal heating at periastron inflates stellar radii, shifting disruption boundaries. Backward integration matches the energy requirements of the Fermi bubbles, and relativistic precession does not suppress mass-ratio inspiral rates, providing a model for event topologies in target galactic nuclei.
AI.conclusion: Space-fractional transport (superdiffusive Lévy processes) is essential for correctly modeling the S-star cluster dynamics around Sgr A*. The framework resolves the Schwarzschild barrier paradox, explains observed flux growth and tidal disruption, connects current phase space configurations to Fermi bubble energetics, and offers a predictive model for extreme mass-ratio inspiral events relevant to space-borne gravitational wave detectors.

title: The influence of feedback on the baryonic content of haloes in the COLIBRE simulations
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: We present predictions for the relation between the halo gas mass fraction and halo mass, $f_{\rm gas}^{200}-M_{200}$, from the COLIBRE cosmological simulations of galaxy formation, and explore how the gas content of haloes is influenced by feedback from supernovae and active galactic nuclei (AGN) over time. The $f_{\rm gas}^{200}-M_{200}$ relation in COLIBRE is non-monotonic, with a peak at $M_{200}\sim 10^{11.5-12}$~M$_\odot$. Below this mass, feedback from supernovae efficiently expels gas from the haloes of dwarf galaxies, and above it, AGN feedback efficiently depletes the haloes of galaxy groups. The fiducial COLIBRE model yields gas fractions for galaxy groups and clusters that agree with constraints from Chandra and XMM-Newton X-ray data, but which are high relative to gas fractions inferred from eROSITA stacks and measurements of the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel-dovich (kSZ) effect. COLIBRE's hybrid AGN feedback model, which combines thermal and jet-driven feedback, produces lower gas fractions in better agreement with eROSITA and kSZ measurements. COLIBRE produces lower gas fractions for groups and clusters than EAGLE and other contemporary simulations, and better agreement with observational constraints. We investigate the origin of this improvement relative to EAGLE, and how the resolution of the simulation affects the impact of feedback. Our results demonstrate that halo gas fractions are a sensitive probe of feedback physics, and that they can differ significantly between simulations that otherwise produce very similar galaxy populations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents predictions for the halo gas mass fraction-halo mass relation from the COLIBRE cosmological simulations, showing a non-monotonic relation peaked at M200~10^11.5-12 M⊙, where SN feedback dominates below and AGN feedback above. COLIBRE's hybrid AGN feedback (thermal + jet) produces lower gas fractions yielding better agreement with eROSITA and kSZ observations than its fiducial model, and outperforms EAGLE and other contemporary simulations.
AI.motivation: To understand how feedback from supernovae and AGN shapes the gas content of haloes across cosmic time, and to demonstrate that halo gas fractions are a sensitive discriminator of feedback physics even between simulations producing similar galaxy populations.
AI.method: Analysis of COLIBRE cosmological simulations, comparing the fgas200-M200 relation against observational constraints from Chandra, XMM-Newton, eROSITA stacks, and kSZ measurements. Systematic comparison with EAGLE and other simulations, including exploration of resolution effects and the relative impact of hybrid (thermal+jet) versus thermal AGN feedback models.
AI.result: COLIBRE's fiducial model matches X-ray (Chandra/XMM) group and cluster gas fractions but overpredicts eROSITA and kSZ constraints. The hybrid AGN feedback model reduces gas fractions to agree with eROSITA/kSZ. COLIBRE yields lower group/cluster gas fractions than EAGLE and other simulations, with better observational agreement. Halo gas fractions differ significantly between simulations with otherwise similar galaxy populations, establishing them as a sensitive probe of feedback.
AI.conclusion: Halo gas mass fractions are a powerful, sensitive diagnostic of feedback physics. The COLIBRE hybrid AGN feedback model provides the best agreement with current observational constraints on halo gas content, improving over EAGLE. The choice of AGN feedback implementation and resolution materially alters predicted gas fractions even when galaxy properties converge.

title: An Exploratory Analysis of New Large Gaia-informed Quasar Samples in SDSS-V
comment: Resubmitted to ApJ on 28 July 2026 after addressing the referee report. The data will be available in SDSS-V/DR20
summary: Quasars are luminous objects that provide insights into the physics and evolution of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their accretion flows, galaxy evolution, and even cosmology. In this study, we present an exploratory study based on the ongoing fifth generation of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-V) and its unique dual-hemisphere, wide-field, and multi-object spectroscopic capabilities, with the aim of creating a comprehensive, all-sky quasar sample. The targets were selected through two novel methods, GUA and Skewt-QSO, that rely primarily on data from WISE and Gaia, aiming to address gaps in previous large quasar samples. Our sample includes over 250,000 spectroscopically confirmed quasars reaching z~5, with tens of thousands of newly identified quasars in the southern hemisphere. The selection methods are highly pure, with well over 80% of the spectra collected being genuine quasars; the main contaminants are M-type stars. The detailed spectral decomposition procedure we employed shows that the quasars in the sample span a wide range of luminosities (Lbol~$10^{44}-10^{48} erg s^{-1}$), SMBH masses (MBH~$10^6-10^{10}$ Msun), and accretion rates (L/LEdd~0.01-1). The distributions of these properties are consistent with those of previous quasar catalogs, which are based on past generations of SDSS, once we account for potential selection biases related to the various survey depths. Our findings confirm that novel selection methods based on optical+IR colors and/or astrometry can yield a large, high-purity quasar sample over wide sky areas, including in cases where more nuanced multi-band photometry and/or multi-wavelength data in the X-ray or radio is not available. This SDSS-V sample, which will continue to grow, establishes a robust reference for future southern (time-domain) surveys, while enhancing and complementing our understanding of quasar demographics and SMBH evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an exploratory study using SDSS-V's dual-hemisphere spectroscopic capabilities to build a comprehensive all-sky quasar sample. Using two novel selection methods (GUA and Skewt-QSO) based on WISE and Gaia data, the sample includes over 250,000 spectroscopically confirmed quasars reaching z~5, with selection purity exceeding 80% (main contaminants being M-type stars). The quasars span broad ranges in luminosity (Lbol~10^44-10^48 erg/s), SMBH mass (10^6-10^10 Msun), and Eddington ratios (~0.01-1), consistent with previous SDSS-based catalogs after accounting for selection biases.
AI.motivation: To create a comprehensive all-sky quasar sample that addresses gaps in previous large quasar catalogs, particularly in the southern hemisphere, using novel selection methods based primarily on optical+IR colors and astrometry from WISE and Gaia rather than relying on extensive multi-wavelength data.
AI.method: Leveraging SDSS-V's dual-hemisphere, wide-field, multi-object spectroscopic capability, the authors selected quasar targets using two novel methods (GUA and Skewt-QSO) that rely on WISE and Gaia data. Spectroscopic confirmation was obtained via SDSS-V, followed by detailed spectral decomposition to derive quasar physical properties including bolometric luminosity, SMBH mass, and accretion rate.
AI.result: The sample contains over 250,000 spectroscopically confirmed quasars up to z~5, including tens of thousands of new southern-hemisphere discoveries. Selection methods achieve >80% purity with M-type stars as the main contaminants. The derived quasar properties span Lbol~10^44-10^48 erg/s, MBH~10^6-10^10 Msun, and L/LEdd~0.01-1, statistically consistent with previous SDSS quasar catalogs once survey-depth selection biases are accounted for.
AI.conclusion: Novel selection methods based on optical+IR colors and/or astrometry can deliver large, high-purity all-sky quasar samples even without X-ray or radio data. The growing SDSS-V quasar sample will serve as a robust reference for future southern time-domain surveys and complement our understanding of quasar demographics and SMBH evolution.

title: Semi-analytic Inference of Satellite Densities in the Cold Dark Matter Model Part II. Implications for Dark Matter Indirect Detection Constraints
comment: 16+9 pages, 4+6 figures, video abstract at https://youtu.be/x9zNkN6XyAA
summary: Dwarf galaxies provide excellent targets to search for signals of dark matter annihilation or decay. Using a calibrated semi-analytic model and the latest stellar kinematic data (presented in Part I), this paper updates the astrophysical J-factors for the Milky Way's dwarf spheroidal galaxies. We infer the probability distributions for the J-factors of 39 dwarfs by conditioning a population of subhalos, generated with the SatGen semi-analytic satellite model, on either a dwarf's kinematically determined dynamical mass or its stellar mass. We also compute the J-factors using the Jeans equation with updated stellar kinematics and priors that incorporate varying degrees of SatGen information. We use the computed J-factors to recast existing limits from Fermi-LAT data on the annihilation cross section. Our main result is that variations in the J-factors computed using the Jeans analysis introduce a factor of 2-4 uncertainty into the inferred limits on the cross section. We argue that a cosmologically informed prior is a motivated choice that excludes thermal relic annihilation cross sections to $b\bar{b}$ below about 70 GeV. For comparison, the more commonly used priors, which can lead to unphysical halo parameters, exclude masses below 130 GeV at 95% confidence level. We also show that the highest-J-factor dwarfs are spatially extended, approximately one degree on the sky, which challenges the validity of the point-source approximation adopted in many analyses of Fermi data. Finally, based on the semi-analytic model and the kinematic data, the highest J-factor halos have already been discovered, suggesting future ultra-faint discoveries are unlikely to substantially strengthen limits on annihilating dark matter.

AI.tldr: This paper updates the astrophysical J-factors for 39 Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies using a calibrated semi-analytic model (SatGen) and the latest stellar kinematic data, then uses these to recast Fermi-LAT limits on dark matter annihilation cross sections. Variations in Jeans-based J-factors introduce factor 2-4 uncertainty in inferred limits; cosmologically informed priors exclude thermal relic annihilation cross sections to b-bbar below ~70 GeV; the highest-J-factor dwarfs are spatially extended (~1 degree), challenging point-source approximations; and future ultra-faint discoveries are unlikely to substantially strengthen annihilation limits.
AI.motivation: Dwarf galaxies are prime targets for probing dark matter annihilation/decay signals, but J-factor uncertainties significantly affect derived limits on dark matter annihilation cross sections. This work aims to improve J-factor estimates using cosmologically motivated priors and updated kinematic data.
AI.method: The authors condition a population of subhalos generated by the SatGen semi-analytic satellite model on either kinematically determined dynamical masses or stellar masses of 39 dwarfs to infer J-factor probability distributions. They also compute J-factors via the Jeans equation with updated stellar kinematics and varying degrees of SatGen-informed priors, then recast Fermi-LAT limits on the annihilation cross section.
AI.result: Variations in Jeans-based J-factors introduce a factor of 2-4 uncertainty in inferred cross-section limits. Cosmologically informed priors exclude thermal relic annihilation to b-bbar below ~70 GeV, whereas common priors (which can yield unphysical halo parameters) exclude masses below 130 GeV at 95% CL. The highest-J-factor dwarfs are spatially extended (~1 degree on sky), challenging point-source assumptions. The highest J-factor halos have already been discovered.
AI.conclusion: Cosmologically motivated priors are a preferred choice for J-factor estimation in dark matter searches; the angular extent of high-J-factor dwarfs necessitates careful treatment beyond the point-source approximation in Fermi data analyses, and the discovery of new ultra-faint dwarfs is unlikely to significantly improve annihilation limits.

title: Exploring the Limits of Spectral Line Stacking in Spectral Line Data and Application Toward the Detection of Bulk $^{13}$C Enrichment of Aromatics in TMC-1
summary: The formation history of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in the interstellar medium remains a topic of active debate, with proposed mechanisms ranging from high-temperature stellar ejecta processes to low-temperature chemistry within molecular clouds. Recently, the identification of small PAHs in the cold, dark cloud TMC-1 has provided some circumstantial evidence of the latter. If these are formed in situ, their isotopic ratios, particularly $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C, should reflect the local, bulk material of the molecular cloud; in contrast, PAHs formed in the circumstellar envelopes of evolved stars may show enhanced $^{13}$C abundances. The expected radio signals of these $^{13}$C substituted species will be faint, and thus we conducted a detailed proof-of-concept analysis examining whether spectral line stacking and matched filtering techniques can robustly retrieve signal from multiple singly substituted $^{13}$C isotopologues in aggregate. We find that while retrieved signal decreases in the limit of spectral line confusion, false-positive detections are exceedingly improbable at the adopted 5$σ$ matched filter response detection threshold. We then demonstrate the technique on actual observational data of isotopologues of HC$_9$N toward TMC-1. Finally, we show using synthetic data that if laboratory rotational spectra of all singly substituted $^{13}$C isotopologues of cyanonaphthalene and cyanopyrene isomers existed, current observations of TMC-1 would be sensitive enough to discriminate between a local, bulk $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio and one with an enhanced $^{13}$C abundance suggestive of inheritance.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a proof-of-concept study on using spectral line stacking and matched filtering to detect faint 13C-substituted PAH isotopologues in cold molecular clouds, demonstrating the technique on HC9N isotopologues in TMC-1 and showing via synthetic data that such observations could discriminate between in situ PAH formation and inheritance from evolved stars based on 12C/13C ratios.
AI.motivation: The formation mechanism of PAHs in the interstellar medium is debated—whether they form in high-temperature stellar ejecta or via low-temperature chemistry in molecular clouds. Detecting 13C isotopologues of PAHs in cold clouds like TMC-1 would provide the isotopic ratio needed to discriminate between these scenarios, but the expected radio signals are extremely faint, motivating a proof-of-concept analysis of signal retrieval techniques.
AI.method: The authors conduct a detailed proof-of-concept analysis examining whether spectral line stacking and matched filtering techniques can robustly retrieve signal from multiple singly substituted 13C isotopologues in aggregate. They analyze detection statistics including false-positive probability at a 5σ matched filter threshold, apply the technique to observational data of HC9N isotopologues toward TMC-1, and use synthetic data to assess sensitivity for cyanonaphthalene and cyanopyrene isomers.
AI.result: Retrieved signal decreases in the limit of spectral line confusion, but false-positive detections are exceedingly improbable at the adopted 5σ matched filter detection threshold. The technique is successfully demonstrated on actual HC9N isotopologue data toward TMC-1. Synthetic data show that if laboratory rotational spectra of all singly substituted 13C isotopologues of cyanonaphthalene and cyanopyrene existed, current TMC-1 observations would be sensitive enough to discriminate between a local bulk 12C/13C ratio and one with enhanced 13C abundance suggestive of inheritance.
AI.conclusion: Spectral line stacking and matched filtering offer a viable path toward detecting faint 13C-substituted PAH isotopologues. With sufficient laboratory spectra, current observational sensitivity toward TMC-1 could distinguish between PAHs formed in situ in the molecular cloud versus those inherited from evolved stellar envelopes, thereby constraining the dominant PAH formation channel in the interstellar medium.

title: Relativistic effects of PSR~J1856--0039 double neutron star system in a 2.36-hour compact orbit
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, accepted by Phys. Rev. Lett
summary: Compact double neutron star (DNS) systems are unique laboratories for testing gravitational theories and studying DNS mergers. Here we report the properties of a new DNS system, PSR J1856--0039, discovered in the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST). The pulsar is mildly recycled with a period of 23.4~ms in a compact eccentric orbit ($e=0.106$) with an orbital period of 2.36 hours. By following up FAST observations, we measured the relativistic effects, including the orbital period derivative $\dot{P}_{\rm orb}=-1.284\pm0.019\times10^{-12}$ s s$^{-1}$, periastron advance $\dotω=17.5859\pm0.0007$ deg yr$^{-1}$, and Einstein delay $γ=0.445\pm0.011$ ms. This DNS system has a low orbital inclination of $i=133^\circ.2\pm1^\circ.1$ and the lowest total mass of any known DNS, $M_{\rm tot}=2.48841\pm0.00015 M\odot$, with a determined pulsar mass of $1.304\pm0.022 M_\odot$ and a companion mass of $1.185\pm0.022 M_\odot$, one of the lowest neutron-star masses. The observed orbital decay due to gravitational-wave emission $\dot{P}^{\rm GW}_{\rm orb,obs}$ and the orbital decay predicted by general relativity $\dot{P}^{\rm GW}_{\rm orb,pred}$ are consistent at a level of $\dot{P}^{\rm GW}_{\rm orb,obs}/\dot{P}^{\rm GW}_{\rm orb,pred}=$1.009(14) (68% confidence). This DNS will merge after 82 Myr and may form a stable neutron star or collapse into a black hole after spin-down. Long-term monitoring could potentially probe the Lense-Thirring precession.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery and characterization of PSR J1856-0039, a new double neutron star system found by FAST. It has the lowest total mass of any known DNS (2.48841 solar masses), a low orbital inclination, and its observed gravitational-wave-induced orbital decay is fully consistent with general relativity predictions. The system will merge in 82 Myr and offers long-term prospects for probing Lense-Thirring precession.
AI.motivation: Compact double neutron star systems serve as unique laboratories for testing gravitational theories and studying DNS mergers. Discovering new DNS systems with precise relativistic parameter measurements enables deeper tests of general relativity and advances our understanding of neutron star masses and evolution.
AI.method: The pulsar PSR J1856-0039 was discovered with the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) and followed up with additional FAST observations. Timing analysis measured relativistic effects including orbital period derivative, periastron advance, and Einstein delay, from which system parameters (masses, inclination, total mass) were derived.
AI.result: The system has a 23.4 ms mildly recycled pulsar in a compact eccentric orbit (e=0.106) with a 2.36-hour orbital period. Measurements yielded total mass of 2.48841 solar masses (the lowest known DNS), pulsar mass of 1.304 solar masses, companion mass of 1.185 solar masses, and orbital inclination of 133.2 degrees. Observed gravitational-wave orbital decay agrees with GR prediction at a ratio of 1.009(14) at 68% confidence. The system will merge in 82 Myr.
AI.conclusion: This new DNS system provides a strong test of general relativity through precise orbital decay measurements, hosts one of the lowest-mass neutron stars known, and offers future prospects for probing Lense-Thirring precession through long-term monitoring. Its merger outcome could be a stable neutron star or black hole after spin-down.

title: Cosmic Pairs: A DESI Census of Dual and Offset AGN as Precursors to Massive Black Hole Binaries
comment: 38 pages, 18 figures, 1 table. To be submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a systematic census of dual and offset active galactic nuclei (AGN) using spectroscopic data from the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). After correcting for observational systematics, our final sample contains $>7,000$ dual AGN and 27,000 galaxy pairs containing one AGN over the redshift range $0 \lesssim z \lesssim 3.6$. This sample expands the known dual AGN sample by $\sim 1-2$ orders of magnitude at $0.2 \lesssim z \lesssim 0.4$, includes $\sim 50$ dwarf dual AGN candidates in a regime where only a handful were previously known, and triples the census at $z>2$. Dual AGN are preferentially found at small separations, consistent with merger-driven triggering of AGN activity. The two members of a pair differ in their star formation response: the more massive (primary) host changes little with separation, while the less massive (secondary) lies $\sim 0.3$ dex above matched inactive and one-AGN companions at the same projected separation in main-sequence offset. Using ASTRID simulations, we predict that the fraction of DESI dual AGN whose central black holes will merge by $z \sim 0$ increases with redshift, reaching $\sim 76\%$ by $z \sim 2$, while the fraction producing LISA-detectable mergers peaks at $\sim 37\%$ near $z \sim 0.9$. These results provide the largest uniformly selected spectroscopic sample of kpc-scale dual and offset AGN candidates from a single survey, connecting their host-galaxy and AGN demographics to the progenitor population of massive black hole mergers detectable by LISA.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the largest uniformly selected spectroscopic sample of dual and offset AGN from DESI DR1, containing >7,000 dual AGN and 27,000 galaxy pairs with one AGN over z~0-3.6, expanding known samples by 1-2 orders of magnitude and connecting their demographics to the progenitor population of massive black hole mergers detectable by LISA.
AI.motivation: The goal is to create a systematic and uniformly selected census of dual and offset AGN — a regime where only small samples existed previously — in order to understand the role of mergers in triggering AGN activity and to connect observed dual AGN populations to the progenitors of massive black hole mergers detectable by gravitational wave observatories like LISA.
AI.method: The authors use spectroscopic data from DESI DR1 to systematically identify dual and offset AGN. They correct for observational systematics and construct a final sample of >7,000 dual AGN and 27,000 single-AGN galaxy pairs across 0<z<3.6. They analyze pair separation statistics, star formation offsets of paired hosts, and use ASTRID simulations to predict black hole merger fractions and LISA-detectable merger rates as a function of redshift.
AI.result: The sample expands known dual AGN by ~1-2 orders of magnitude at 0.2<z<0.4, includes ~50 dwarf dual AGN candidates, and triples the census at z>2. Dual AGN are preferentially found at small separations, consistent with merger-driven triggering. The secondary (less massive) hosts show ~0.3 dex elevated star formation above matched controls, while primaries show little change. ASTRID simulations predict 76% of DESI dual AGN central black holes will merge by z~0 at z~2, with LISA-detectable merger fractions peaking at ~37% near z~0.9.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the largest uniformly selected spectroscopic sample of kpc-scale dual and offset AGN from a single survey, demonstrating merger-driven AGN triggering and asymmetric star-formation responses in paired hosts, and connecting these systems to the progenitor population of LISA-detectable massive black hole mergers.

title: Exploring cosmic magnetism with gamma-ray burst afterglow emission
summary: The nature and origin of magnetic fields on cosmological scales are still unclear. Magnetic fields detected in galaxies and galaxy clusters are typically interpreted as the result of the amplification of weak seed fields, but their nature remains largely unknown with two scenarios considered: the cosmological and the astrophysical origin. Signatures of magnetization in cosmic voids from observations of very high energy (VHE, E > 100 GeV) photons from extragalactic sources can provide crucial results. Indeed, if a non-negligible intergalactic magnetic field (IGMF) is present in the voids, a time-delayed emission known as pair-echo is expected. The timing and intensity of this signal encode information on the IGMF strength B and properties. Given the recent detection of GRB afterglows at TeV energies, in this article we perform a detectability study of pair-echo signatures from GRBs. We simulate afterglow emission for different values of the jet kinetic energy (E$_{k,iso}$ = 10$^{49}$ - 10$^{55}$ erg), redshift (z = 0.03 - 1), and lightcurve break times, and estimate the expected pair-echo radiation for IGMF strengths in the range B = 10$^{-19}$ - 10$^{-16}$ G. We investigate the capability of CTAO to detect the resulting emission at tens of GeV. We find that a subsample of GRBs in the z - E$_{k,iso}$ parameter space can produce a detectable pair-echo component for CTAO for all the tested IGMF strengths. A steepening of the GRB afterglow light curve, caused e.g. by an early (0.1 - 1 days) jet break, is a key factor to increase the chances of detection. CTAO observations starting from 10 - 12 hrs up to a few days after the GRB trigger time can provide relevant results to probe IGMF.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the detectability of pair-echo signatures from gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) with the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) to probe the intergalactic magnetic field (IGMF). The authors simulate GRB afterglow emissions across a wide parameter space (jet kinetic energy, redshift, lightcurve break times) and estimate pair-echo radiation for IGMF strengths of 10^-19 to 10^-16 G, finding that a subsample of GRBs can yield detectable pair-echo components, particularly when the afterglow light curve exhibits an early jet break.
AI.motivation: The nature and origin of magnetic fields on cosmological scales remain unclear. Detecting magnetization signatures in cosmic voids through pair-echo emission from very high energy photons can provide crucial constraints on the intergalactic magnetic field (IGMF). Recent detections of GRB afterglows at TeV energies motivate assessing whether GRB pair-echoes are detectable with upcoming instruments.
AI.method: The authors simulate GRB afterglow emission for jet kinetic energies E_k,iso = 10^49 - 10^55 erg, redshifts z = 0.03 - 1, and various lightcurve break times. They estimate the expected pair-echo radiation for IGMF strengths B = 10^-19 - 10^-16 G and investigate CTAO's capability to detect the resulting emission at tens of GeV.
AI.result: A subsample of GRBs in the z - E_k,iso parameter space can produce a detectable pair-echo component for CTAO across all tested IGMF strengths. A steepening of the GRB afterglow light curve, caused by an early (0.1-1 days) jet break, significantly increases detection chances. CTAO observations starting 10-12 hours up to a few days after the GRB trigger can yield relevant results.
AI.conclusion: GRB pair-echo signatures represent a promising observational avenue to probe the IGMF with CTAO, provided observations commence within roughly 10-12 hours after the GRB trigger and persist for several days. Early jet breaks in the afterglow lightcurve are a key factor for maximizing detection probability across all tested IGMF strengths.

title: Stellar photoionisation modelling in SYNTHESIZER
comment: 29 pages and 29 figures. Submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: Emission from photoionised gas surrounding young stellar populations ($H\text{II}$ regions) provides critical diagnostics of the physical conditions in star forming galaxies. This emission constrains the gas properties, the nature of ionising sources, and generates essential features for determining galaxy redshifts. To leverage spectroscopic observations to test galaxy formation models, it is essential to incorporate these emissions into synthetic datasets. Here, we present the integration of photoionised gas emission into the SYNTHESIZER package (https://synthesizer-project.github.io) and demonstrate its application. We quantify the impact of key modelling assumptions - including stellar population synthesis models, initial mass functions, ionisation parameter, gas density, geometry, abundance pattern, elemental depletion, and dust - on spectral diagnostics. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of SYNTHESIZER through its application in different scenarios ranging from exploring emission in toy parametric models to large-volume cosmological simulations with realistic star formation and metal enrichment histories. Taken together, SYNTHESIZER provides a flexible, physically motivated framework to model stellar and nebular emissions, serving as a vital link between theory and observations in the era of next-generation spectroscopic missions.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the integration of photoionised gas (H II region) emission into the SYNTHESIZER package, a Python framework for modelling stellar and nebular emission from star-forming galaxies. It quantifies the impact of key modelling assumptions on spectral diagnostics and demonstrates applications ranging from toy models to large-volume cosmological simulations.
AI.motivation: Emission from photoionised gas surrounding young stellar populations provides crucial diagnostics of physical conditions in star-forming galaxies, constraining gas properties, ionising source nature, and enabling galaxy redshift determination. To test galaxy formation models with spectroscopic observations, these emissions must be incorporated into synthetic datasets, motivating the integration of this capability into SYNTHESIZER.
AI.method: The authors integrated photoionised gas emission into the SYNTHESIZER package and quantified the impact of key modelling assumptions—including stellar population synthesis models, initial mass functions, ionisation parameter, gas density, geometry, abundance pattern, elemental depletion, and dust—on spectral diagnostics. They demonstrated versatility by applying SYNTHESIZER across scenarios from toy parametric models to large-volume cosmological simulations with realistic star formation and metal enrichment histories.
AI.result: SYNTHESIZER now provides a flexible, physically motivated framework capable of modelling both stellar and nebular emissions, validated through applications spanning toy models and full cosmological simulations.
AI.conclusion: SYNTHESIZER serves as a vital link between theory and observations in the era of next-generation spectroscopic missions, enabling comprehensive modelling of star-forming galaxy spectra.

title: Binary neutron star populations across cosmic time: the impact of binary stellar evolution uncertainties
summary: We investigate the impact of uncertainties in binary stellar evolution on the formation efficiency and cosmological merger rate of BNS systems. In particular, we aim to determine whether robust signatures of binary evolution can be identified across a broad range of metallicities. We perform a systematic exploration of 72 binary evolution models using the population synthesis code COSMIC. We vary four key parameters controlling the onset and efficiency of common-envelope evolution, the natal kick prescription, and the treatment of kicks during the common envelope phase. For each model, we compute the BNS formation efficiency and cosmological merger rate using several prescriptions for the cosmic metallicity-redshift relation. We identify characteristic features in the metallicity dependence of the BNS formation efficiency that arise from specific evolutionary processes. These include the onset of first-giant-branch skipping at low metallicity and a non-monotonic evolution between $Z=10^{-3}$ and $7.5\times 10^{-3}$. All models also predict a bimodal distribution of BNS progenitor masses associated with two distinct formation channels. The common envelope ejection efficiency and natal kick prescription remain the dominant sources of uncertainty, producing variations of several orders of magnitude in both the BNS formation efficiency and the cosmological merger rate. Finally, we show that different combinations of binary-evolution parameters can produce similar merger-rate histories, highlighting significant degeneracies among population-synthesis models. Current gravitational-wave observations can rule out only the least efficient formation scenarios. Breaking these degeneracies will require larger samples of BNS mergers expected from future third-generation gravitational-wave observatories, and improved observational constraints on the evolution of metallicity across cosmic time.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically explores 72 binary stellar evolution models using COSMIC to investigate how uncertainties in binary evolution parameters affect BNS formation efficiency and cosmological merger rates across metallicities. They identify characteristic metallicity-dependent features and bimodal progenitor mass distributions, finding that common-envelope efficiency and natal kick prescriptions are the dominant uncertainty sources. They also highlight significant parameter degeneracies that current gravitational-wave observations cannot fully break.
AI.motivation: To determine whether robust signatures of binary evolution can be identified across a broad range of metallicities, and to quantify how uncertainties in key binary stellar evolution parameters impact BNS formation efficiency and cosmological merger rate predictions.
AI.method: A systematic exploration of 72 binary evolution models using the population synthesis code COSMIC. Four key parameters were varied: (1) the onset and efficiency of common-envelope evolution, (2) the natal kick prescription, and (3) the treatment of kicks during the common-envelope phase. BNS formation efficiency and cosmological merger rates were computed for each model using several cosmic metallicity-redshift relation prescriptions.
AI.result: Characteristic features in the metallicity dependence of BNS formation efficiency arise from specific evolutionary processes, including first-giant-branch skipping onset at low metallicity and non-monotonic evolution between Z=10^-3 and 7.5x10^-3. All models predict a bimodal progenitor mass distribution from two distinct formation channels. Common-envelope ejection efficiency and natal kick prescription dominate uncertainties, producing several orders of magnitude variation in both efficiency and merger rates. Different parameter combinations can yield similar merger-rate histories, and current gravitational-wave observations can only rule out the least efficient formation scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Significant degeneracies exist among population-synthesis models in predicting BNS merger rates. Breaking these degeneracies requires larger BNS merger samples from future third-generation gravitational-wave observatories and improved observational constraints on metallicity evolution across cosmic time.

title: Galactic HII regions in LAMOST Medium-Resolution Spectroscopic Survey of Nebulae
summary: Based on LAMOST Medium-Resolution Spectroscopic Survey of Nebulae (MRS-N) data and WISE Galactic HII region catalog, we construct a sample of 280 Galactic HII regions and candidates in the Outer Galaxy (80$^{\circ}$ $\lesssim$ l $\lesssim$ 220$^{\circ}$). Using MRS-N optical spectra, we measure four emission lines (H$α$, [NII]$λ$6584, [SII]$λλ$6717,6731) and use line-ratios to spectroscopically confirm 255 HII regions, including 90 previously "Known" HII regions and 165 newly classified ones. We measure their $T_{\rm e}$, $n_{\rm e}$ and oxygen abundance, and determine distances via associated OB stars and the kinematic method. The sample spans $R_{\rm gal}$ from 8.16 to 15.36 kpc, enabling investigation of radial gradients in physical properties. We find [NII]/H$α$ and [SII]/H$α$ decrease with increasing $R_{\rm gal}$, while [SII]/[NII] remains nearly flat; these trends are quite different from diffuse ionized gas (DIG). We derive the $T_{\rm e}$ gradient of 344.530 $\pm$ 78.083 K kpc$^{-1}$, and the $\log n_{\rm e}$ gradient of -0.143 $\pm$ 0.041 cm$^{-3}$ kpc$^{-1}$. Oxygen abundance shows a steep slope of -0.044 $\pm$ 0.010 dex kpc$^{-1}$ in the inner disk and a shallow slope of -0.016 $\pm$ 0.005 dex kpc$^{-1}$ in the outer disk, with a global slope of -0.014 $\pm$ 0.005 dex kpc$^{-1}$. We also examine the two-dimensional distributions of $T_{\rm e}$, $n_{\rm e}$, and oxygen abundance, and find the gradients vary with azimuth. There is no obvious difference between spiral arm and interarm regions, and no trend appears along individual arms. From [NII]/H$α$-[SII]$λ$6717/H$α$ diagram, HII regions have a S$^+$/S ratio (0.32), lower than DIG (0.43); however, heavy overlap prevents clear separation from this diagram alone.

AI.tldr: An analysis of 280 Galactic HII regions and candidates in the Outer Galaxy using LAMOST MRS-N optical spectra, spectroscopically confirming 255 regions and measuring their electron temperature, density, and oxygen abundance. The sample reveals radial gradients in physical properties, including a Te gradient of 344.5 K/kpc and oxygen abundance slopes that steepen in the inner disk, with azimuth-dependent variations but no spiral arm differences.
AI.motivation: To construct a large sample of Galactic HII regions in the Outer Galaxy using LAMOST medium-resolution spectra, spectroscopically confirm their nature, and systematically investigate radial gradients of physical properties (temperature, density, metallicity) across a wide galactocentric radius range (8.16-15.36 kpc), which is key for understanding Galactic chemical evolution and disk structure.
AI.method: Cross-matched LAMOST MRS-N survey data with the WISE Galactic HII region catalog to build a sample of 280 HII region candidates in the Outer Galaxy (80° ≤ l ≤ 220°). Measured four optical emission lines (Hα, [NII]λ6584, [SII]λλ6717,6731) and used line-ratio diagnostics for spectroscopic confirmation. Derived electron temperature (Te), electron density (ne), and oxygen abundances, with distances determined from associated OB stars and kinematic methods. Analyzed radial gradients, two-dimensional distributions, azimuthal variations, and compared HII regions with diffuse ionized gas (DIG) using diagnostic diagrams.
AI.result: Confirmed 255 HII regions (90 previously known, 165 newly classified) from 280 candidates. Found [NII]/Hα and [SII]/Hα decrease with galactocentric radius while [SII]/[NII] stays flat, differing from DIG. Derived Te gradient of 344.5±78.1 K/kpc and log ne gradient of -0.143±0.041 cm⁻³/kpc. Oxygen abundance shows a steep inner-disk slope (-0.044±0.010 dex/kpc) and shallow outer-disk slope (-0.016±0.005 dex/kpc) with global slope of -0.014±0.005 dex/kpc. Gradients vary with azimuth; no differences between spiral arm and interarm regions. HII regions have lower S⁺/S ratio (0.32) than DIG (0.43), but significant overlap prevents clear separation.
AI.conclusion: The Outer Galaxy HII region sample reveals distinct radial gradients in physical properties that differ from the inner disk and from diffuse ionized gas. The steep-to-shallow oxygen abundance slope transition suggests a flattening metallicity gradient in the outer disk, while azimuthal variations in gradients indicate the need for three-dimensional treatment of Galactic chemical evolution.

title: Radio Follow-Up of Einstein Probe Fast X-Ray Transients
summary: Fast X-ray transients (FXTs) are brief, luminous bursts of soft X-ray emission whose physical origins remain uncertain. The Einstein Probe (EP) mission has recently enabled prompt discovery of these events, providing opportunities for rapid multi-wavelength follow-up. We present a coordinated radio observing campaign targeting 20 FXTs detected by the EP in 2024. The core consists of 59 epochs with the Allen Telescope Array (ATA), sampling post-burst timescales from $\sim$1 to $\sim$65 days and reaching typical $3σ$ sensitivities of 0.6--1.5\,mJy across 1--8\,GHz. Two FXTs---EP240315a and EP241021a---have radio counterparts. For EP241021a, AMI-LA monitoring at 15.5\,GHz reveals a light curve peaking at $\sim$30 days with $F_ν\approx1.0$\,mJy; equipartition analysis implies a Newtonian equipartition energy of $\sim3\times10^{49}$\,erg and a mildly relativistic on-axis solution with $Γ_{\rm on}\approx1.3$. Multi-frequency modelling of EP240315a, combining new VLA measurements with published MeerKAT, ATCA, and eMERLIN data, indicates highly relativistic early emission ($Γ\gtrsim3$) that decelerates with time, consistent with jetted outflow. The detections and ATA non-detections span luminosities overlapping the brightest GRB and relativistic tidal disruption event (TDE) afterglows, suggesting FXTs comprise a heterogeneous population including both relativistic and non-relativistic explosions. Under a GRB-like redshift prior, our $3σ$ ATA limits correspond to observer-frame specific-luminosity thresholds of $\sim10^{32}$--$10^{33}\,\mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}\ Hz^{-1}}$; for nearby events ($z\lesssim0.2$), $L_ν\lesssim10^{30\text{--}31}\,\mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}\ Hz^{-1}}$. Planned ATA upgrades and next-generation arrays (SKA, DSA, ngVLA) will enable sensitive, population-level radio studies of the FXT radio sky.

AI.tldr: A coordinated radio observing campaign of 20 Fast X-ray Transients (FXTs) detected by the Einstein Probe in 2024, using the Allen Telescope Array and other facilities, found radio counterparts for two events (EP240315a and EP241021a) with properties suggesting FXTs comprise a heterogeneous population of both relativistic and non-relativistic explosions.
AI.motivation: FXTs are poorly understood brief X-ray bursts of uncertain origin, and the Einstein Probe mission now enables prompt discovery and rapid multi-wavelength follow-up. Radio observations are needed to constrain their physical nature, energetics, and relationship to GRBs and TDEs.
AI.method: A coordinated radio campaign targeting 20 FXTs with 59 epochs from the Allen Telescope Array (1-8 GHz, ~1-65 days post-burst), supplemented by AMI-LA 15.5 GHz and multi-frequency VLA, MeerKAT, ATCA, and eMERLIN observations for detected events, with equipartition and light-curve modeling.
AI.result: Two radio counterparts found. EP241021a shows a light curve peaking at ~30 days with ~1 mJy, implying Newtonian equipartition energy ~3x10^49 erg and mildly relativistic outflow (Gamma~1.3). EP240315a exhibits highly relativistic early emission (Gamma>=3) decelerating over time, consistent with a jetted outflow. Detections and non-detections span luminosities overlapping bright GRB and relativistic TDE afterglows, indicating a heterogeneous FXT population.
AI.conclusion: FXTs are a heterogeneous source class including both relativistic and non-relativistic explosions. ATA limits set luminosity thresholds of ~10^32-10^33 erg/s/Hz under GRB-like priors. Upcoming facilities (SKA, DSA, ngVLA, ATA upgrades) will enable sensitive population-level radio studies of FXTs.

title: The X-ray-Weak Tail of the Quasar Population: Physical Properties and Redshift Evolution of Variability-Selected AGN in eFEDS
summary: (abridged) Aims: To characterize variability-selected AGN candidates within the eROSITA Final Equatorial-Depth Survey (eFEDS), leveraging the synergy between optical variability and deep X-ray observations by SRG (Spectrum Roentgen Gamma)/eROSITA, to compare the physical properties of AGN populations selected through complementary methods. Methods: We used a sample of AGN candidates selected via optical variability by Arévalo et al. and cross-match it to the X-ray selected eFEDS AGN sample. Spectroscopic characterizations are obtained for the matched samples from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument public data products. Results: We find a high classification purity with 98% candidates confirmed as broad-line AGN/QSOs. We identify a significant population (25%) that lack X-ray counterparts (X-U) in the eFEDS survey. We find that the X-D and X-U samples exhibit distinct physical properties and redshift distributions. The X-U sample peaks at $z = 2$ while the X-D sample at $z =1$, with nearly half of the variability-selected AGN at $z > 2.5$ remaining undetected in X-rays. This missing fraction can be attributed to K-correction effects and SED evolution with luminosity, mainly resulting in high accretion rate objects falling out of the X-D sample at higher redshifts. X-ray variability accounts for a part of the missing fraction but its dependence with redshift is less clear. Ensemble spectral analysis reveals that X-D sources have steeper optical continua and stronger broad emission lines than their X-U counterparts, while the forbidden and semi-forbidden lines have equal EWs in both samples. Finally, broad absorption line (BAL) features are found almost exclusively in the X-U population. This "missing" X-ray population must be accounted for when extrapolating X-ray-selected AGN to the broader Type I population and could impact cosmic estimates of massive black hole growth.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes variability-selected AGN candidates in the eFEDS survey by cross-matching optical variability-selected AGNs with deep eROSITA X-ray observations. The sample shows 98% classification purity as broad-line AGNs, but 25% lack X-ray counterparts. X-ray-detected and X-ray-undetected populations differ in physical properties and redshift distributions, with missing X-ray sources peaking at z=2 and attributable mainly to K-correction and SED evolution effects, plus BAL features found almost exclusively in the X-ray-undetected population.
AI.motivation: To characterize variability-selected AGN candidates in eFEDS by leveraging the synergy between optical variability and deep X-ray observations, and to compare physical properties of AGN populations selected through complementary selection methods to understand what fraction of the Type I AGN population is missed by X-ray surveys and the implications for cosmic black hole growth estimates.
AI.method: The authors cross-matched a sample of optically variability-selected AGN candidates (from Arévalo et al.) with the X-ray-selected eFEDS AGN sample from SRG/eROSITA. Spectroscopic characterization was obtained from DESI public data products for matched samples.
AI.result: 98% of variability-selected candidates confirmed as broad-line AGN/QSOs. 25% lack X-ray counterparts (X-U). X-U sample peaks at z=2 while X-D peaks at z=1, with ~half of variability-selected AGN at z>2.5 undetected in X-rays. Missing fraction attributed to K-correction and SED evolution with luminosity, mainly high accretion rate objects falling out at high redshifts. X-ray variability plays a secondary role. X-D sources show steeper optical continua and stronger broad emission lines; BAL features found almost exclusively in X-U population.
AI.conclusion: The missing X-ray population must be accounted for when extrapolating X-ray-selected AGN to the broader Type I population, as it could impact cosmic estimates of massive black hole growth.

title: On the triple nature of the PSR J0435+3233 system
summary: Context. The recent pulsar timing ephemeris of PSR J0435+3233 indicates that this millisecond pulsar (MSP) has a spin-down rate that is much higher than observed in other MSPs and challenges our understanding of the formation and evolution of MSPs. Aims. We propose that this system is a hierarchical triple, and that the high spin-down rate is caused by varying acceleration due to a tertiary in a wide orbit. Methods. We use pulsar timing methods with radio and gamma-ray observations of PSR J0435+3233 to determine the system properties. Results. We find that a hierarchical triple timing model describes the timing observations of PSR J0435+3233 and that this results in the detection of gamma-ray pulsations back to the beginning of the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) data in 2008. The intrinsic spin-down rate remains uncertain as it correlates with the parameters of the outer orbit, but large spin-down rates are excluded and the intrinsic rate is at least two orders of magnitude lower than the observed rate, in line with other Galactic MSPs. We identify a star located 11 mas from the pulsar position as the optical counterpart to the tertiary companion. From the 1.5-2.5 kpc distance and colours, we infer that the tertiary is a 1.2 solar mass F-type main-sequence star. Along with the pulsar binary, it orbits the common centre of mass with an eccentric (e ~ 0.6), wide (~ 70 yr) orbit that is likely seen at a low orbital inclination. Conclusions. We conclude that PSR J0435+3233 is a hierarchical triple system. We discuss the motivation and prospects for the continued study of this system. Spectral measurements of the outer star in addition to continued astrometric measurements will yield mass ratio and inclination estimates, while continued pulsar timing may yield a tighter constraint on violations of the Strong Equivalence Principle than are currently obtained from PSR J0337+1715.

AI.tldr: PSR J0435+3233, previously thought to have an anomalously high spin-down rate for a millisecond pulsar, is shown to be a hierarchical triple system. The high apparent spin-down is due to acceleration from a wide-orbit tertiary (a 1.2 solar mass F-type main-sequence star on an eccentric ~70 yr orbit). Once modeled as a triple, gamma-ray pulsations are detected back to 2008, and the intrinsic spin-down rate drops to at least two orders of magnitude lower, consistent with other Galactic MSPs.
AI.motivation: The observed spin-down rate of PSR J0435+3233 is much higher than typical millisecond pulsars, challenging current understanding of MSP formation and evolution. The authors propose a hierarchical triple explanation to resolve this discrepancy.
AI.method: The authors use pulsar timing techniques with both radio and gamma-ray (Fermi-LAT) observations to test a hierarchical triple timing model for PSR J0435+3233, determine the system's orbital parameters, and identify the optical counterpart of the tertiary companion.
AI.result: A hierarchical triple timing model fits the observations, enabling detection of gamma-ray pulsations back to 2008. The intrinsic spin-down rate is at least two orders of magnitude lower than observed and consistent with other Galactic MSPs. An F-type main-sequence star (~1.2 solar masses) located 11 mas from the pulsar is identified as the tertiary, orbiting on an eccentric (e~0.6), wide (~70 yr) orbit likely seen at low inclination, at a distance of 1.5-2.5 kpc.
AI.conclusion: PSR J0435+3233 is confirmed as a hierarchical triple system. Future spectral and astrometric measurements of the outer star will constrain the mass ratio and inclination, while continued pulsar timing may provide tighter Strong Equivalence Principle violation constraints than currently available from PSR J0337+1715.

title: Revealing the Physical Driver of the Baldwin Effect: Gas Density in the Broad-Line Region
comment: Comments: 11 pages, 7 figures, 4 appendix figures. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The Baldwin effect --- the inverse correlation between the equivalent width of emission lines and the continuum luminosity in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) --- has been known for nearly five decades, yet its physical origin remains poorly understood. Using a sample of 41,159 radio quasars constructed from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Low-Frequency Array Two-metre Sky Survey, we investigate the origin and underlying physics of the Baldwin effect of MgII broad emission lines in both radio-quiet (RQ) and radio-loud (RL) quasars. We find that the slope $β$ of the Baldwin effect is positively correlated with the Eddington ratio $λ_{\rm Edd}$ in both populations, and RL quasars exhibit steeper $β$ than their RQ quasars at fixed $λ_{\rm Edd}$. Photoionization simulations reveal that the $β$ is primarily governed by the gas density in the broad-line region (BLR): lower gas densities yield steeper slopes. This density-driven mechanism naturally connects the Baldwin effect to the broader AGN evolutionary context. Specifically, higher $λ_{\rm Edd}$ drive stronger accretion disk winds, leading to denser BLRs and shallower $β$. Our findings indicate that BLR gas density serves as the primary physical driver underlying the "global" Baldwin effect, offering a physically grounded framework for interpreting AGN accretion states and their coupled evolution with host galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the physical origin of the Baldwin effect (inverse correlation between emission-line equivalent width and continuum luminosity) in MgII broad lines using 41,159 radio quasars from SDSS and LoTSS. The authors find the Baldwin effect slope β correlates positively with Eddington ratio in both radio-quiet and radio-loud quasars, with RL quasars showing steeper slopes. Photoionization simulations show β is governed primarily by BLR gas density, where lower gas densities produce steeper slopes. This density-driven mechanism links the Baldwin effect to AGN evolution via accretion disk winds.
AI.motivation: The Baldwin effect has been known for nearly five decades, yet its physical origin remains poorly understood. This paper aims to unravel the underlying physics driving this phenomenon using a large sample of radio quasars and identify the primary physical driver.
AI.method: Using 41,159 radio quasars from SDSS and LoTSS, the authors analyze the Baldwin effect slopes (β) of MgII broad emission lines in both radio-quiet and radio-loud quasars. They correlate β with Eddington ratio and employ photoionization simulations to determine the physical parameter governing the slope.
AI.result: The Baldwin effect slope β is positively correlated with Eddington ratio in both RQ and RL quasars, and RL quasars show steeper β than RQ at fixed λ_Edd. Photoionization simulations reveal β is primarily governed by BLR gas density: lower gas densities produce steeper slopes.
AI.conclusion: BLR gas density serves as the primary physical driver of the "global" Baldwin effect. Higher Eddington ratios drive stronger accretion disk winds leading to denser BLRs and shallower β, providing a physically grounded framework connecting AGN accretion states with host galaxy evolution.

title: JWST Spectra Indicate a Large Mass of Postshock Dust Formed by SN 2010jl
summary: We present new JWST mid-IR spectra and ground-based optical spectra of the lingering source at the position of SN 2010jl, which was a relatively nearby superluminous Type IIn supernova having strong interaction with circumstellar material (CSM). Early-time data showed evidence of dust, interpreted as either pre-existing CSM dust, or as newly formed dust in the SN ejecta and post-shock region. At 13 yr post explosion, JWST reveals a strong MIR excess from warm dust, with broad features at 10-15 $μ$m. Our analysis reveals a minimum dust mass of $>$0.11 $M_{\odot}$, and a more likely value of 0.2 $M_{\odot}$ or more because the dust is optically thick. This is among the largest masses of SN-produced dust yet measured without far-IR/submm data, and greatly exceeds SN 2010jl's dust mass inferred around 2-3 yr post-explosion. Ground-based optical spectra confirm the presence of a young massive cluster at the SN position, and confirm that blueshifted line profiles persisting until the latest epochs arise from dust formed in the post-shock region. The warmest dust emitting in the MIR is likely to be the same post-shock dust causing the blueshift. The JWST spectrum also reveals silicate absorption, which may arise from cool SN ejecta dust along the line of sight to the receding shock. The large mass of post-shock dust in SN 2010jl suggests that strong CSM interaction promotes efficient dust production, where the new post-shock dust will survive. If strongly interacting SNe are common in the early Universe, this may contribute significantly to dust seen in infant galaxies.

AI.tldr: New JWST mid-IR and ground-based optical spectra of SN 2010jl at 13 years post-explosion reveal a large mass of warm dust (>0.11 M⊙, likely ~0.2 M⊙ or more) with broad 10-15 μm features and silicate absorption. The dust is predominantly formed in the post-shock region, and blueshifted line profiles confirm this origin. This represents one of the largest SN-produced dust masses measured, suggesting strong CSM interaction promotes efficient and surviving dust production with implications for dust in early-Universe galaxies.
AI.motivation: To determine the amount and origin of dust in SN 2010jl, a strongly interacting Type IIn supernova, at 13 years post-explosion, addressing the long-standing question of whether supernovae can produce and retain substantial dust masses, and whether strongly interacting SNe can contribute to dust seen in infant galaxies.
AI.method: JWST mid-infrared spectroscopy combined with ground-based optical spectroscopy of the lingering source at the SN 2010jl position. The MIR spectrum was used to model warm dust emission and derive dust mass constraints, while optical spectra confirmed the presence of a young massive cluster and traced the temporal evolution of blueshifted line profiles.
AI.result: The analysis finds a minimum dust mass of >0.11 M⊙, with a more likely value of 0.2 M⊙ or more given significant optical depth. This is among the largest SN-produced dust masses measured without far-IR/submm data and exceeds earlier estimates from 2-3 years post-explosion. The blueshifted line profiles confirm post-shock dust formation, and silicate absorption suggests cool SN ejecta dust along the line of sight to the receding shock.
AI.conclusion: Strong CSM interaction in superluminous SNe like SN 2010jl promotes efficient dust production, and the newly formed post-shock dust can survive. If such strongly interacting SNe were common in the early Universe, they could significantly contribute to the dust observed in infant galaxies.

title: The eROSITA X-ray luminosity function of active galactic nuclei
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures. Catalogue including redshift information is released via the eROSITA web pages and CDS upon the journal's article acceptance
summary: The X-ray luminosity function (XLF) of active galactic nuclei (AGN) provides an observational probe of the growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) across cosmic time. With its large survey grasp, Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG)/eROSITA samples the luminosity--redshift plane with a depth--area balance complementary to pencil-beam surveys, providing the volume needed to detect rare luminous AGN, previously limited by small-number statistics. We measure the soft XLF, leveraging an eROSITA sample spanning approximately eight orders of magnitude in luminosity out to $z\simeq6$. This enables us to study luminosity-dependent evolution with improved constraints, and to infer both the SMBH accretion history and optical/UV missed AGN population. We introduce a new redshift-dependent smoothly broken power-law parameterisation in which all XLF model parameters are allowed to evolve continuously with redshift. We find lower space densities for moderately and very luminous AGN at low redshift, while the abundance is higher than previously found at the highest redshifts. Comparisons to optical/UV quasar LFs converted to rest-frame $2\!-\!10\,\mathrm{keV}$ show that the UV-missed fraction decreases with luminosity, and, in the most luminous bin, increases with redshift. Integrating the XLF yields a black-hole accretion-rate density peaking at $z \simeq 1.5$, with the corresponding cumulative black-hole mass density indicating $\sim80^{+11}_{-23}\%$ obscured growth relative to locally-inferred BH mass estimates derived from scaling relations and missed by the soft X-ray selection of our sample. With this work, we release the eROSITA DR2 AGN catalogue, including counterparts and their redshift information. We then discuss how these results can inform future spectroscopic, photometric, and X-ray survey strategies aimed at improving AGN demographic constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the soft X-ray luminosity function (XLF) of AGN using the SRG/eROSITA sample spanning ~8 orders of magnitude in luminosity out to z~6, introducing a new redshift-dependent smoothly broken power-law parameterization. The authors find lower space densities for luminous AGN at low redshift but higher abundances at high redshift, quantify the UV-missed AGN fraction, and infer that ~80% of black hole growth is obscured relative to local estimates.
AI.motivation: To leverage eROSITA's large survey grasp to extend AGN XLF measurements with a depth-area balance complementary to pencil-beam surveys, overcoming small-number statistics that previously limited constraints on rare luminous AGN and enabling studies of luminosity-dependent evolution, SMBH accretion history, and the obscured/UV-missed AGN population.
AI.method: Measure the soft XLF from an eROSITA AGN sample spanning ~8 decades in luminosity to z~6. Introduce a new redshift-dependent smoothly broken power-law parameterization in which all XLF model parameters evolve continuously with redshift. Compare to optical/UV quasar luminosity functions converted to rest-frame 2-10 keV, integrate the XLF to derive black-hole accretion-rate density, and release the eROSITA DR2 AGN catalogue with counterparts and redshifts.
AI.result: Lower space densities for moderately and very luminous AGN at low redshift, but higher abundances at high redshift than previously found. The UV-missed fraction decreases with luminosity and increases with redshift in the most luminous bin. The black-hole accretion-rate density peaks at z~1.5, with cumulative black-hole mass density indicating ~80(+11/-23)% obscured growth relative to locally-inferred BH mass estimates from scaling relations.
AI.conclusion: The results inform future spectroscopic, photometric, and X-ray survey strategies aimed at improving AGN demographic constraints, and highlight the significant fraction of obscured SMBH growth missed by soft X-ray selection.

title: Depolarization Induced by Rapid Polarization Angle Swings: A Common Feature of Pulsars and Fast Radio Bursts?
summary: The polarization angle (PA) of pulsars and fast radio bursts (FRBs) provides a useful diagnostic of the magnetic fields in their emission regions and is therefore crucial for understanding their radiation and origins. Within a general geometric framework for polarized emission from a rotating neutron star, we suggest a possible anti-correlation between the degree of linear polarization $Π_\text{L}$ and $d\text{PA}/dt$, the time derivative of the PA, as a common feature of pulsars and FRBs. The depolarization arises from the incoherent superposition of radiation with different polarization directions within the observable part of the emission region, and is detectable only when the PA swing is steep enough. We test this conjecture using a sample of radio pulsars and find possible evidence for the expected anti-correlation in a subset of pulsars. Whether this relation holds in FRBs remains uncertain due to limited observational data. Identification of this feature would not only provide insights into the rotating magnetospheric origin of FRBs, but also place constraints on the spin periods and geometric parameters of the neutron stars that power these mysterious bursts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a physical mechanism linking polarization angle (PA) swing rate to depolarization in pulsars and fast radio bursts (FRBs). Within a geometric framework for polarized emission from a rotating neutron star, the authors suggest an anti-correlation between the degree of linear polarization and the time derivative of PA, arising from incoherent superposition of differently polarized radiation. They find tentative evidence for this in a subset of radio pulsars, while FRB confirmation remains uncertain but would constrain neutron star spin periods and geometry.
AI.motivation: PA is a critical diagnostic of magnetic fields in emission regions of pulsars and FRBs, and understanding the relationship between polarization properties and PA evolution could reveal the physical origins of these sources, particularly whether FRBs arise from rotating magnetospheres.
AI.method: A general geometric framework is developed for polarized emission from a rotating neutron star. The model predicts depolarization from incoherent superposition of radiation with differing polarization directions across the observable emission region, detectable only when the PA swing is steep. The prediction is tested against a sample of radio pulsars to look for an anti-correlation between linear polarization degree and dPA/dt.
AI.result: Possible evidence for the predicted anti-correlation between Π_L and dPA/dt is found in a subset of radio pulsars. For FRBs, the relation remains unconfirmed due to limited observational data.
AI.conclusion: If confirmed, this anti-correlation feature would support a rotating magnetospheric origin for FRBs and provide constraints on neutron star spin periods and geometric parameters powering the bursts.

title: Invariant manifolds in barred galaxy simulations. III. Self-regulated weakening of strong spiral arms
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in A&A on 30/07/2026
summary: We investigated the origin of the weakening of strong spiral arms in barred galaxies, seeking the physical mechanism responsible for the decline in the fraction of manifold-trapped particles over time. We reconstructed the gravitational potential of a fully self-consistent N-body simulation of a barred galaxy using AGAMA, computed the Lagrangian points, and quantified how their spiral-induced angular displacement affects the geometry of the invariant manifolds and the associated orbital flows. We find that sufficiently strong, self-gravitating spiral arms significantly reshape the gravitational potential of a barred galaxy, displacing the equilibrium points up to 20-50° from the bar major axis, where they are expected to lie in the standard invariant-manifold framework. This shift alters the configuration of the manifold branches and disrupts the coherent stellar flows that sustain the spiral structure. As the spiral weakens, the equilibrium points gradually return to their standard configuration, restoring the conditions for manifold-driven spiral arm formation on a timescale of ~200 Gyr. We show for the first time that invariant manifolds and the spiral structures they generate are coupled through a self-regulating feedback mechanism, allowing the spiral pattern to recur over time. Our results therefore indicate that, although barred galaxies may sustain spiral activity over long timescales, individual episodes of strong spiral arms are intrinsically transient.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why strong spiral arms in barred galaxies weaken over time by examining how the spirals reshape the galactic potential, displacing Lagrangian equilibrium points by 20-50° from their standard position on the bar major axis. This displacement disrupts the invariant manifolds and coherent stellar flows sustaining the spiral. As spirals weaken, the equilibrium points return to standard configuration over ~200 Gyr, revealing a self-regulating feedback loop between manifolds and spiral arms that explains spiral recurrence while individual episodes remain transient.
AI.motivation: The authors seek the physical mechanism responsible for the time-decline in the fraction of manifold-trapped particles and the consequent weakening of strong spiral arms in barred galaxies.
AI.method: They reconstruct the gravitational potential of a fully self-consistent N-body barred galaxy simulation using AGAMA, compute the Lagrangian equilibrium points, and quantify how spiral-induced angular displacement affects the geometry of invariant manifolds and associated orbital flows.
AI.result: Strong self-gravitating spiral arms significantly reshape the potential, displacing equilibrium points 20-50° from the bar major axis. This shift disrupts manifold branch configurations and coherent stellar flows. As spirals weaken, equilibrium points return to standard configuration over ~200 Gyr, enabling manifold-driven spiral formation to recur.
AI.conclusion: Invariant manifolds and spiral structures are coupled via a self-regulating feedback mechanism that allows spiral patterns to recur over long timescales; however, individual strong spiral episodes are intrinsically transient.

title: An extra hard spectral component peaking at sub-GeV in the prompt emission of GRB 260226A
summary: The prompt emission spectra of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) have long been empirically described by the Band function over the keV--MeV range, whereas several \textit{Fermi}/LAT-detected GRBs show evidence for an extra hard component at higher energies. Here we present a joint GBM--LAT study of GRB~260226A, a rare LAT seeded onboard trigger GRB, and find that an extra sub-GeV component is present. In the time-resolved analysis, we find that a cutoff power-law model fits the spectral data of the extra component better than other models at earlier times, while at later times, the broken power-law model is preferred (or at least equally good). Interpreting the early cutoff as the $γγ$ absorption implies that the Lorentz factor at early time is lower and increases with time. The low ratio between the peak energy of the extra component and that of the Band component is difficult to explain with a one-zone synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) scenario. Two-zone emission models, such as external inverse Compton scattering of the photosphere emission by relativistic electrons accelerated in internal shocks, could provide a possible explanation.

AI.tldr: A joint GBM-LAT spectral analysis of GRB 260226A reveals an extra sub-GeV component beyond the standard Band function. The extra component evolves from a cutoff power-law at early times to a broken power-law at later times. The early cutoff is interpreted as gamma-gamma absorption with a low, increasing Lorentz factor, and the low peak-energy ratio disfavors a one-zone SSC scenario, suggesting two-zone emission models like external inverse Compton of photosphere emission.
AI.motivation: Standard gamma-ray burst prompt spectra are described by the Band function over keV-MeV, but Fermi/LAT-detected GRBs sometimes show an additional hard component at higher energies, warranting case studies to understand its origin and evolution.
AI.method: Joint time-resolved GBM-LAT spectral analysis of GRB 260226A (a rare LAT seeded onboard trigger), fitting the extra sub-GeV component with various models including cutoff power-law and broken power-law, and testing interpretations via gamma-gamma absorption, one-zone SSC, and two-zone emission scenarios.
AI.result: An extra sub-GeV component is confirmed. A cutoff power-law fits better at early times, while a broken power-law is preferred or equally good at later times. The early cutoff interpreted as gamma-gamma absorption implies a lower Lorentz factor that increases with time. The low peak-energy ratio between the extra and Band components cannot be explained by one-zone SSC.
AI.conclusion: Two-zone emission models, such as external inverse Compton scattering of photosphere emission by relativistic electrons accelerated in internal shocks, provide a plausible explanation for the observed extra sub-GeV component in GRB 260226A.

title: A search for HI absorption in distant star-forming galaxies with ASKAP-FLASH - II. Direct observations and stacking of 21 cm line
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present results of a search for associated and intervening HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming galaxies and a control sample of radio galaxies at 0.4 < $z$ < 1.0, using ASKAP's FLASH HI 21 cm absorption survey. We report the detection of a new HI 21 cm absorption line in radio galaxy NVSS J214954-004657 at $z_{\mathrm{HI}}$ = 0.863.
