Additionally, we present results of HI 21 cm stacking for associated and intervening star-forming and radio galaxy catalogues. For the first time at these redshifts, we report tentative detections of stacked HI 21 cm absorption for associated galaxies when stacked in order of descending radio source brightness, and show that these tentative detections become buried as optical depth increases as progressively weaker sources are co-added into the stack. No stacked signal is detected when co-adding intervening galaxy spectra. We speculate that the ability to detect a stacked HI 21 cm detection is dependent on the background source optical depth limits, as well as source covering factors. Covering factor has a greater impact when stacking intervening systems, and can be considered to effectively weaken the observed flux density of a radio source. We find no significant difference in detection rate for associated HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming galaxies versus the general radio-source population at the same redshift. Although detection rates are low, from a meta-analysis of HI 21 cm surveys we find that 1 detection is expected given the survey parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a search for HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming and radio galaxies at 0.4 < z < 1.0 using ASKAP's FLASH survey, reporting one new detection (NVSS J214954-004657 at z=0.863) and tentative stacked absorption detections for associated galaxies ordered by radio brightness, while finding no stacked signal for intervening systems. The detectability depends on optical depth limits and covering factors, with no significant difference in detection rate between star-forming and general radio-source populations.
AI.motivation: To investigate HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming and radio galaxies at intermediate redshifts (0.4 < z < 1.0), exploring both associated and intervening absorption, and to assess the feasibility and detection efficiency of stacking techniques for these populations at these redshifts.
AI.method: The authors used ASKAP's FLASH HI 21 cm absorption survey to search for associated and intervening absorption in star-forming galaxies and a control sample of radio galaxies. They report individual detections and perform stacking analysis for associated and intervening star-forming/radio galaxy catalogues, ordering stacks by radio source brightness, and conduct a meta-analysis of HI 21 cm survey detection expectations.
AI.result: One new HI 21 cm absorption detection (NVSS J214954-004657) at z=0.863. Tentative stacked detections for associated galaxies when stacked by descending radio brightness, which become buried with increasing optical depth as weaker sources are added. No stacked signal from intervening galaxies. No significant detection-rate difference between star-forming and general radio-source populations. The meta-analysis predicts ~1 detection, consistent with observations.
AI.conclusion: The detectability of stacked HI 21 cm absorption depends on background source optical depth limits and covering factors, with covering factor more strongly affecting intervening systems by reducing effective flux density. Detection rates remain low for associated absorption in star-forming galaxies, consistent with expectations from survey meta-analysis.

title: On the Blueprint of Active Galaxies Producing Neutrinos
summary: Based on the observation of the active galaxies NGC 1068 and TXS 0506+056, and on additional evidence for the sources NGC 4151, CGCG 420-015, NGC 7469, and the Circinus Galaxy emerging from IceCube data, we make the case for the production of high-energy neutrinos within a few gravitational radii of supermassive black holes surrounded by a dense plasma radiating X-rays. X-rays represents the target for the production of neutrinos by protons accelerated near the black hole; they also absorb the gamma rays from the decay of neutral pions produced in the same interactions. Neutrinos with energies of tens of TeV and above originate in photoproduction interactions with X-rays of $0.1 \sim 1$\,keV energy on the $Δ$ resonance, $p + γ\rightarrow Δ\rightarrow n + π^+$. Our analysis of the multimessenger data points to gamma-ray-obscured sources with a characteristic neutrino flux linearly proportional to the X-ray flux originating within $\sim 10$ gravitational radii of the black holes, with lower values preferred. We speculate on such sources producing the diffuse flux of neutrinos and cosmic rays of extragalactic origin.

AI.tldr: Based on active galactic nuclei observations (NGC 1068, TXS 0506+056) and additional IceCube evidence, the paper argues that high-energy neutrinos are produced within a few gravitational radii of supermassive black holes surrounded by X-ray-emitting dense plasma, where X-rays serve both as targets for neutrino-producing photoproduction and as absorbers of accompanying gamma rays.
AI.motivation: To explain the origin of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos detected by IceCube by connecting them to active galactic nuclei with gamma-ray-obscured, X-ray-bright environments near supermassive black holes, potentially accounting for the diffuse extragalactic neutrino and cosmic-ray flux.
AI.method: Multimessenger analysis of IceCube neutrino data combined with observations of AGNs (NGC 1068, TXS 0506+056, plus supporting sources), modeling neutrino production via photoproduction interactions with 0.1-1 keV X-rays on the Δ resonance (p + γ → Δ → n + π+), in a region within ~10 gravitational radii of the black hole.
AI.result: The data point to gamma-ray-obscured AGN sources with a characteristic neutrino flux linearly proportional to the X-ray flux originating within ~10 gravitational radii of the black holes, with smaller radii preferred.
AI.conclusion: X-ray-luminous AGN coronae near supermassive black holes are likely sources of high-energy neutrinos, and such obscured sources may account for the diffuse flux of extragalactic neutrinos and cosmic rays.

title: Angular Momentum Evolution from Core to Disk Scales in the Early Phase of Star Formation: Constraints from HH 212, HH 211, and B335
summary: I investigate the angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in the early phase of star formation using three protostellar systems: HH 212, HH 211, and B335. Observations show that the specific angular momentum follows a power-law dependence at core scales and transitions to an approximately constant value at smaller radii, indicating dynamical collapse in the inner envelope. I model this behavior using the inside-out collapse solution of Shu (1977) and its rotating extension, the Terebey-Shu-Cassen model, including modest magnetic effects through a flattened, magnetized core. I find that the observed angular momentum profiles in all three sources are broadly consistent with an inside-out collapse scenario with approximate conservation of specific angular momentum in the collapsing region. The inferred collapse ages and mass infall rates yield total masses accreted onto the center that are broadly consistent with the central masses derived from kinematics, allowing for a fraction of the material to be ejected by jets and winds. The predicted midplane densities at typical radii, including the effect of magnetic flattening, are also consistent with observational estimates. The three systems exhibit a similar pattern of angular momentum evolution despite large differences in the magnitude of their specific angular momentum. In particular, the small disk in B335 can be naturally explained by its lower initial specific angular momentum, although alternative explanations, such as magnetic braking or different initial conditions, cannot be excluded. These results suggest that inside-out collapse, with modest magnetic modification, provides a plausible first-order description of angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in the early phase of star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in early star formation using three protostellar systems (HH 212, HH 211, B335). The observed angular momentum profiles are broadly consistent with inside-out collapse (Shu 1977) and its rotating Terebey-Shu-Cassen extension with modest magnetic flattening. Inferred collapse ages and infall rates match central masses from kinematics, and predicted midplane densities agree with observations. The small disk in B335 is naturally explained by lower initial specific angular momentum.
AI.motivation: To understand how angular momentum evolves from core scales to disk scales during the early phase of star formation, by testing whether a simple inside-out collapse scenario with modest magnetic modification can explain observations across multiple protostellar systems with different properties.
AI.method: The author models angular momentum evolution using the inside-out collapse solution of Shu (1977) and its rotating extension (Terebey-Shu-Cassen model), incorporating modest magnetic effects through a flattened, magnetized core. The model is compared against observational angular momentum profiles from three protostellar systems (HH 212, HH 211, and B335), and used to infer collapse ages, mass infall rates, accreted masses, and midplane densities.
AI.result: All three sources show angular momentum profiles broadly consistent with inside-out collapse with approximate conservation of specific angular momentum in the collapsing region. Inferred collapse ages and mass infall rates yield total accreted masses consistent with kinematic central masses (allowing for jet/wind ejection). Predicted midplane densities including magnetic flattening match observations. A common pattern of angular momentum evolution emerges despite large differences in magnitude. B335's small disk is naturally explained by its lower initial specific angular momentum.
AI.conclusion: Inside-out collapse with modest magnetic modification provides a plausible first-order description of angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in early star formation. Alternative explanations such as magnetic braking or different initial conditions cannot be entirely excluded for the B335 disk case.

title: Distinct Jet Properties in the X-Ray-Obscured State of GRS 1915+105
comment: This is a revised manuscript submitted to ApJ
summary: GRS 1915+105 has remained in an X-ray-obscured state since its transition from a long-lasting unobscured state in 2019. We report on 6.7-GHz East Asia VLBI Network observations of GRS 1915+105 obtained during strong radio flares detected at 2.3--11.2 GHz with the RATAN-600 radio telescope in 2025. Our images reveal two contrasting jet morphologies. The first epoch, associated with a flare evolving from an optically thick to an optically thin spectrum, shows a bright radio core accompanied by an extended jet structure. By contrast, the second epoch, observed near the peak of another flare displaying optically thin emission at lower frequencies, is dominated by two bright, symmetric, well-separated jet blobs and shows no detectable radio core. If these jets exhibited the apparent superluminal motions commonly observed prior to 2019, measurable angular shifts would be expected over the five-hour observations. However, no significant jet motion is detected. Combined with our derived jet speed of $βΓ\lesssim 0.40$, these results suggest that the jets launched during the current obscured state are slower than the relativistic jets ($βΓ\gtrsim 1$) observed earlier during the unobscured state. Together with the recently reported large variations in jet orientation, our findings in GRS 1915+105 provide robust support for the emerging paradigm that X-ray binary jets launched in obscured and unobscured states likely exhibit distinct propagation properties.

AI.tldr: Two high-resolution radio observations of GRS 1915+105 during 2025 flares reveal contrasting jet morphologies (core+extended jet vs. twin symmetric blobs) with no detectable proper motion, implying jet speeds of βΓ≲0.40. This indicates jets in the current obscured state are slower than the relativistic jets (βΓ≳1) seen before 2019, supporting a paradigm where X-ray binary jets differ between obscured and unobscured states.
AI.motivation: GRS 1915+105 entered an X-ray-obscured state in 2019 after a long unobscured phase. This study aims to characterize jet properties during the obscured state and test whether jet kinematics differ fundamentally from those observed pre-2019.
AI.method: 6.7-GHz East Asia VLBI Network imaging of GRS 1915+105 during strong radio flares detected by RATAN-600 across 2.3–11.2 GHz. Two observing epochs captured jet morphology and proper motion, from which jet speed (βΓ) was derived.
AI.result: Epoch 1 shows a bright core with an extended jet during an optically thick-to-thin transition. Epoch 2 shows two bright, symmetric, well-separated jet blobs with no detectable core during optically thin emission. No significant jet motion over five-hour observations yields βΓ≲0.40, slower than the relativistic jets (βΓ≳1) seen in the pre-2019 unobscured state.
AI.conclusion: Jets launched in the current obscured state are sub-relativistic and kinematically distinct from the relativistic jets of the prior unobscured state. Combined with reported jet orientation variations, this supports the emerging paradigm that X-ray binary jets exhibit different propagation properties depending on the obscuration state.

title: Bipolar HII regions Produced by Cloud-Cloud Collisions
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, 1 table, submitted to MNRAS
summary: We use numerical experiments to explore two possibilities: (i) that Bipolar H II Regions are the result of Cloud-Cloud Collisions (CCCs), and (ii) that -- when allowance is made for the chaotic nature of such collisions, the short duration of the bipolar phase, and different viewing angles -- a large proportion of all H II Regions might be the aftermath of CCCs. To reduce the parameter space, our experiments only consider head-on collisions between two $500$ M$_\odot$ clouds, with three different levels of turbulence, and two different collision velocities; the collision velocities define the `collision axis'. In all experiments, OB stars only condense out after a Shock-Compressed Layer has formed (perpendicular to the collision axis), and fragmented to produce a Hub Filament System, with the OB stars forming in the Hub. Ionising radiation from the OB stars excites an H II Region, which tends to expand more rapidly in directions close to the collision axis, and more slowly in directions orthogonal to the collision axis, where it encounters the dense gas of the Shock-Compressed Layer. Consequently, the H II Region may appear bipolar, for a short period during its evolution, if observed at sufficiently large angle to the collision axis. Viewed from smaller angles, the waist appears as a Bright-Rim, similar to conventional approximately spherical H II Regions. Under this circumstance, there are other metrics -- based on the extent of diffuse freefree emission, the velocity dispersion of Radio Recombination Lines, dust emission at mid-infrared wavelengths -- that might indicate the aftermath of a CCC, and establish CCCs as a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper uses numerical simulations of head-on cloud-cloud collisions (CCCs) between two 500 M_sun clouds to show that bipolar H II regions can form as a consequence of such collisions. The simulations reveal that OB stars form in a Hub-Filament System within a shock-compressed layer, and the resulting H II region expands faster along the collision axis, appearing bipolar only when viewed at large angles to that axis. Viewed along the collision axis, the region appears as a conventional spherical H II region with a bright rim. The authors propose additional observational metrics (diffuse free-free emission extent, radio recombination line velocity dispersion, mid-IR dust emission) that could reveal CCC aftereffects, suggesting CCCs may be a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.
AI.motivation: To test whether bipolar H II regions can be explained by cloud-cloud collisions, and to explore whether a large fraction of all H II regions might be the aftermath of such collisions when accounting for chaotic collisions, short bipolar phase duration, and varying viewing angles.
AI.method: Numerical experiments of head-on collisions between two 500 M_sun clouds with three turbulence levels and two collision velocities. The simulations track the formation of shock-compressed layers, Hub-Filament Systems, OB star formation, and subsequent H II region evolution from different viewing angles.
AI.result: OB stars form only after shock-compressed layer fragmentation produces a Hub-Filament System. The H II region expands faster along the collision axis and slower perpendicular to it (due to dense shock-compressed gas), producing a bipolar morphology visible only for a short period at large viewing angles to the collision axis. At smaller angles, the region appears as conventional spherical H II region with a bright-rimmed waist.
AI.conclusion: Bipolar H II regions can result from CCCs, and given the right viewing conditions, many apparently normal H II regions may also be CCC aftermaths. Additional observational diagnostics (diffuse free-free emission extent, RRL velocity dispersion, MIR dust emission) could identify CCC signatures and establish cloud-cloud collisions as a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.

title: eRASSU J043115.8-711730: The first pulsating symbiotic super-soft X-ray source in the Magellanic Bridge
summary: The Magellanic Bridge stellar population is a relic of the tidal interaction between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. A comprehensive view of the evolution of the Bridge stellar population requires probing the compact remnants of stellar evolution, otherwise hidden at optical wavelengths. The all-sky survey conducted by the eROSITA instrument on-board the Spectrum Roentgen Gamma observatory has discovered a significant population of compact-object-powered systems in the Bridge using X-ray. The candidate super-soft source eRASSU J043115.8-711730 (hereafter J0431-71) was discovered as a part of this campaign, and we present here a deeper study of this source using XMM-Newton and SALT spectroscopy, long-term optical-infrared photometry using OGLE, ATLAS, ASAS-SN, WISE, and GAIA data. J0431-71 is a highly variable super-soft X-ray source, classified as a red giant with the GAIA color-magnitude diagram. The source exhibits: (a) a thermal X-ray spectrum with a temperature of kT$\sim$30 eV and a bright state luminosity of $3.2\times10^37$~erg~s$^{-1}$ in the 0.15-1 keV band, (b) Balmer emission lines, [Fe X] coronal line, HeII emission, and the Bowen fluorescence blend, (c) an optical and infrared periodicity of $\sim$500-560 days in phase with the X-ray-UV emission, (d) a 'redder-when-brighter' trend in the stellar emission with a $\sim$520 day period indicating a pulsating donor star. We argue that the observed spectral and temporal properties in J0431-71 are consistent with a high-accretion rate onto a white-dwarf via Roche-lobe overflow, making J0431-71 the first symbiotic source discovered in the Bridge.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-wavelength study of the super-soft X-ray source eRASSU J043115.8-711730 (J0431-71), discovered in the Magellanic Bridge by eROSITA. Using XMM-Newton, SALT spectroscopy, and long-term optical-IR photometry (OGLE, ATLAS, ASAS-SN, WISE, GAIA), the authors characterize it as a highly variable super-soft source with a ~30 eV thermal X-ray spectrum, optical emission lines (Balmer, [Fe X], HeII, Bowen fluorescence), and ~500-560 day optical/IR periodicity. They conclude it is a symbiotic system with a white dwarf accreting at high rate via Roche-lobe overflow from a pulsating red giant donor — the first symbiotic source discovered in the Magellanic Bridge.
AI.motivation: To fully understand the stellar evolution of the Magellanic Bridge population, it is necessary to probe compact remnants of stellar evolution, which are hidden at optical wavelengths. This study aims to characterize compact-object-powered systems in the Bridge using X-ray and multi-wavelength follow-up, specifically focusing on the newly discovered candidate super-soft source J0431-71.
AI.method: Deep multi-wavelength study combining XMM-Newton X-ray spectroscopy, SALT optical spectroscopy, and long-term optical/infrared photometry from OGLE, ATLAS, ASAS-SN, WISE, and GAIA to characterize the spectral and temporal properties of J0431-71.
AI.result: J0431-71 is a highly variable super-soft X-ray source with a thermal spectrum (kT~30 eV) and bright-state luminosity of 3.2×10^37 erg/s in 0.15-1 keV. It exhibits Balmer, [Fe X], HeII, and Bowen fluorescence lines, a ~500-560 day optical/IR periodicity in phase with X-ray-UV emission, and a 'redder-when-brighter' trend with ~520 day period indicating a pulsating donor. The white dwarf accretes at high rate via Roche-lobe overflow from a red giant donor.
AI.conclusion: J0431-71 is confirmed as the first symbiotic source discovered in the Magellanic Bridge, with properties consistent with high-accretion-rate white dwarf via Roche-lobe overflow. This fills a gap in understanding the evolution of compact binary systems in the Bridge stellar population.

title: Searching in HI for Massive Low Surface Brightness Galaxies: II. Completing the UGC Sample
summary: Although Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxies are increasingly well studied, considerable uncertainty still exists as to both their range in properties and their evolutionary history. LSB galaxies provide a fascinating extreme in galaxy formation and evolution, allowing excellent tests of galaxy formation and evolution theories. Previously, our group successfully measured the HI gas and dynamical mass properties of 350 LSB galaxies, significantly increasing the number of known extreme LSB galaxies (massive, gas rich, etc.) in the process. Here we oresent 100-m Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope 21-cm HI line observations of a further 35 LBG galaxies, only two of which have previously published data. Of the 35, 19 were detected. This paper also includes the HI information for five additional galaxies detected accidentally (in the blank sky region or at alternative velocities), none of which has previously published HI results.

AI.tldr: This paper presents new 21-cm HI line observations of 35 Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxies using the 100-m Green Bank Telescope, detecting 19 of them, plus 5 serendipitous detections, expanding the known sample of extreme LSB galaxies.
AI.motivation: LSB galaxies remain poorly understood in terms of their property ranges and evolutionary histories, and they serve as excellent testbeds for galaxy formation and evolution theories. The authors aim to expand the sample of known extreme LSB galaxies (massive, gas-rich) to better constrain these theories.
AI.method: The authors used the 100-m Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope to conduct 21-cm HI line observations of 35 LSB galaxies, only two of which had previously published data. They also report HI information for five additional galaxies detected serendipitously.
AI.result: Of the 35 targeted LSB galaxies, 19 were detected in HI. Additionally, five galaxies were detected accidentally in blank sky regions or at alternative velocities, none of which had previously published HI results.
AI.conclusion: This work continues the group's effort to significantly increase the number of known extreme LSB galaxies with measured HI gas and dynamical mass properties, providing further observational constraints for galaxy formation and evolution theories.

title: Comprehensive X-ray Study of Giant Radio Galaxies with XMM-Newton and Chandra
comment: Accepted for publication in JHEAp , 21 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables
summary: We present a systematic X-ray spectral analysis of 27 giant radio galaxies (GRGs) using archival \textit{XMM-Newton} and \textit{Chandra} data. Roughly 44\% of the sample show intrinsic absorption ($N_{\mathrm{H,int}} \gtrsim 10^{21}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$), while several exhibit narrow Fe K$α$ emission lines with equivalent widths up to $\sim$570 eV. Soft X-ray features are also common, including thermal plasma emission (kT$\sim 0.2$--0.8 keV) and ionized absorbers, in some cases consistent with high-velocity outflows. The photon indices are typically hard (median $ Γ\sim 1.6$), in line with radio-loud AGN. A comparison between nuclear X-ray luminosity and extended radio power shows that many sources host relatively strong X-ray cores compared to their lobes, pointing toward possible restarted nuclear activity. For 10 GRGs with published black hole masses, we explore preliminary relations with X-ray luminosity, Eddington ratio, and photon index. We find a positive trend between $M_{\rm BH}$ and $L_{2-10\,{\rm keV}}$, while Eddington ratios show no clear dependence on mass. A tentative negative relation between $λ_{\rm Edd}$ and $Γ$ hints at inefficient accretion, although confirmation will require larger samples. Overall, GRGs display diverse nuclear conditions and accretion states, supporting scenarios where obscuration, episodic or restarted activity, and low-efficiency accretion shape their long-term evolution.

AI.tldr: A systematic X-ray spectral analysis of 27 giant radio galaxies reveals that ~44% show intrinsic absorption, several exhibit narrow Fe Kα lines, and many have soft X-ray features like thermal plasma and ionized outflows. The authors find typically hard photon indices, relatively strong X-ray cores, and preliminary relations between black hole mass, X-ray luminosity, Eddington ratio, and photon index, supporting scenarios of obscuration, restarted activity, and low-efficiency accretion.
AI.motivation: To systematically characterize the nuclear X-ray properties of giant radio galaxies (GRGs) — the largest radio structures in the universe — in order to understand their accretion states, obscuration properties, and long-term evolution, as these objects remain poorly studied compared to their smaller radio-loud counterparts.
AI.method: The authors performed a systematic X-ray spectral analysis of 27 GRGs using archival XMM-Newton and Chandra data. X-ray spectra were modeled to measure intrinsic absorption, Fe Kα emission lines, soft X-ray thermal plasma, ionized absorbers/outflows, and photon indices. They compared nuclear X-ray luminosities to extended radio powers and explored correlations between black hole mass, 2-10 keV luminosity, Eddington ratio, and photon index for a subsample of 10 GRGs with published BH masses.
AI.result: ~44% of the sample exhibit intrinsic absorption (N_H,int ≳ 10^21 cm^-2); several show narrow Fe Kα lines with EWs up to ~570 eV; thermal plasma (kT~0.2-0.8 keV) and ionized absorbers/outflows are common; photon indices are hard (median Γ~1.6); many sources have relatively strong X-ray cores vs. their lobes; a positive trend between M_BH and L_2-10 keV is found, no clear mass dependence for Eddington ratios, and a tentative negative λ_Edd–Γ correlation is observed.
AI.conclusion: GRGs display diverse nuclear conditions and accretion states. Their properties support the idea that obscuration, episodic/restarted activity, and low-efficiency accretion jointly shape the long-term evolution of these giant radio galaxies, though larger samples are needed to confirm the tentative scaling relations.

title: JWST's Constraints on the Substellar IMF in NGC 2024
summary: A recent study has reported the detection of a turnover in the initial mass function (IMF) below 12 Mjup and the possible detection of a minimum mass near 3 Mjup in the heavily embedded cluster NGC 2024 (<1 Myr), which was based on a sample of brown dwarf candidates in NIRCam images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). I have used those NIRCam data in conjunction with archival spectra from JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) to constrain the substellar IMF in NGC 2024. I present NIRSpec data for 87 sources, 67 of which are within the NIRCam field. Based on those spectra and data from previous studies (e.g., X-ray emission), I have classified 45 of the NIRSpec targets as members of NGC 2024, 17 of which have spectral types indicative of brown dwarfs (M6.5-L; 13 are within NIRCam). The latter have mass estimates as low as 4 Mjup according to theoretical evolutionary models. There remain a few photometric candidates lacking spectra that extend down to the completeness limit of the images (>=2 Mjup for Ak>=1), so the minimum mass of the IMF has not been detected. It is not possible to measure a reliable substellar IMF from the NIRCam images because of the small number of brown dwarfs encompassed by them, a bias against objects at lower masses due to the high extinctions, and incompleteness at >=10 Mjup due to the saturation limit. Thus, there is no evidence in the JWST data for a turnover below 12jup.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines the substellar IMF in NGC 2024 using JWST NIRSpec spectra of 87 sources (67 in the NIRCam field), classifying 45 as cluster members, of which 17 are brown dwarfs (M6.5-L) with masses as low as ~4 Mjup. The author finds no evidence for an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup, as previously claimed, because the NIRCam sample is too small, biased against low-mass objects by high extinction, and incomplete at high masses due to saturation.
AI.motivation: To test the recently claimed detection of an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup and a possible minimum mass near 3 Mjup in NGC 2024, using spectroscopic follow-up of the photometric brown dwarf candidates.
AI.method: Combined JWST NIRCam photometry with archival NIRSpec spectra for 87 sources (67 within the NIRCam field). Classified cluster membership using spectra plus ancillary data (e.g., X-ray emission), derived spectral types, and estimated masses using theoretical evolutionary models.

title: The SRG/eROSITA All-Sky Survey DR2: Cumulative X-ray catalogues from the first three surveys and multi-wavelength counterparts in the western Galactic hemisphere
comment: 24 pages, 12 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A. Accompanying eROSITA-DE Data Release 2
summary: The eROSITA telescope array on board the Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) mission began its all-sky survey program in December 2019, scanning the sky at an approximately six-month cadence. Here, we present new catalogues of point-like and extended X-ray sources derived from the first three completed eROSITA all-sky surveys (eRASS:3), covering the western Galactic hemisphere, which Germany's eROSITA consortium holds proprietary rights for. We describe the observational strategy, data processing, and analysis pipelines. We also characterise the resulting X-ray source populations. The eRASS:3 main catalogue contains nearly two million sources, including 1,911,744 point-like and 63,796 extended sources, detected in the 0.2-2.3 keV energy band, eROSITA's most sensitive energy window. This volume has doubled the X-ray source content of eRASS1 and provides a comprehensive census of X-ray-emitting objects across diverse astrophysical classes. We also released a secondary hard catalogue of nearly 15,000 sources detected in the harder 2.3-5.0 keV energy band. In addition, we released six catalogues, three for the main sample and three for the hard sample, in which we identify and classify the optical and infrared counterparts of eRASS:3 point-like sources. This approach delivers a homogeneous, high-quality identification of mostly extragalactic X-ray emitters; for example, we estimate that approximately 88% of the 1.4 million counterparts identified within the footprints of the Legacy Survey Imaging for DESI are extragalactic sources. This work has enabled the generation of samples optimised for completeness and purity, while expanding the discovery space for rare populations. The second data release (DR2) of the SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey is a catalogue-only release, comprising the catalogues presented in this work together with an updated version of the eROSITA upper flux limit server.

title: X-ray Absorption Variability in NGC 1142: Another Constraint on the Nature of the Torus/Broad-Line Region in Active Galactic Nuclei
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: The physics, geometry, and kinematics of the gas and dust surrounding the central engine of active galactic nuclei (AGN) are not well understood. In some sources, this material obscures the coronal X-ray emission, allowing its line-of-sight column density ($N_H$) to be measured. Many sources display $N_H$ variability across multiple epochs. Studying this variability can provide information about the distribution and dynamics of the obscuring material. Particularly, previous works have shown that the probability of observing $N_H$ variability increases with the number of observations available. Additionally, the observed magnitudes of the $N_H$ variability depend on the timescale between observations. In this work, we present the $N_H$ variability analysis of NGC 1142, which has a total of nine X-ray observations over $\sim20$ years, including five from a NuSTAR+XMM-Newton monitoring campaign performed in 2024-2025 and reported here for the first time. We use the physically-motivated torus models UXCLUMPY, XSKIRTor, and RXTorusD to model the spectra. Our results confirm the previously observed trends, and we compare these trends to simulated obscuration curves assuming different locations and distributions of obscuring clouds.

title: Thermal or Non-thermal? Diffuse emission in the infall region of stacked galaxy groups
comment: Submitted to A&A, 12 pages, 5 figures, 1 table
summary: The faint infall regions surrounding the virial radius of galaxy groups remain largely unexplored due to their low X-ray surface brightness. Using the large statistical power of SRG/eROSITA survey observations, we present the first spectroscopic measurement of the intragroup medium (IGrM) in the infall regions of a large sample of low-mass galaxy groups ($M_{\rm tot}<1\times10^{14}\,M_{sun}$), extending to $\sim2\,R_{200m}$ (2.2 Mpc). Through spectral stacking of 827 nearby groups from the first eROSITA All-Sky Survey catalog, we detect diffuse emission and measure the thermodynamic properties of gas at densities previously inaccessible to X-ray observations. The stacked spectra are well described by a Gaussian differential emission measure model, yielding a temperature distribution with a mean temperature of $0.96_{-0.04}^{+0.05}$ keV and width of $0.28_{-0.10}^{+0.10}$ keV, and a metal abundance of $0.21_{-0.04}^{+0.06}$ A$_{sun}$, consistent with expectations for group outskirts. The inferred electron densities decrease from $(4.8\pm1.3)\times10^{-5}$cm$^{-3}$ at $(0.7-2)\,R_{500c}$ to $(5.5\pm2.0)\times10^{-6}$ cm$^{-3}$ at $(2-4)\,R_{500c}$, demonstrating eROSITA's ability to probe the low-density outskirts of galaxy groups. Residual emission in the spectra suggests the presence of an additional spectral component. While a secondary thermal interpretation requires an unexpectedly hot, metal-poor plasma, a non-thermal inverse Compton model provides an equally plausible explanation, contributing $\sim30\%$ of the thermal flux. Assuming that the additional component is produced by inverse Compton emission from a common population of relativistic electrons, the inferred magnetic field strength would be in the sub-$μ$G regime.

title: Characterizing the disruption of Böotes III: a missing link in the Galactic halo?
summary: The Böotes III (Boo3) dwarf galaxy has long been suspected of being the progenitor of Styx, a ~50°-long stellar stream that was simultaneously discovered in the same region of sky. Boo3's diffuse morphology, large velocity dispersion, small pericenter, and excess of candidate stars at large radii suggest it is undergoing active tidal disruption. A link to Styx is therefore logical; however, a clear connection between these structures has not yet been clearly demonstrated. Here, we re-examine the Boo3-Styx association by searching for Boo3's tidal debris using a combination of Gaia-selected members, new CaHK narrow-band imaging with CFHT/MegaCam, and stellar tracer catalogues of blue horizontal branch and red giant branch stars. We also conduct a broad search for a putative stream using matched filter techniques applied to SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2. Despite our extensive search, we find no observational evidence directly linking Boo3 to Styx. Furthermore, our results suggest that either Boo3's extended substructure is too diffuse to be detected with current data, or that its particular orbit may have erased a coherent tidal signature. Boo3 thus remains an enigmatic system, and exemplifies the need for spectroscopic follow-up to properly disentangle the nature between this faint Milky Way satellite and nearby stream.

title: Tidal Disruption Events with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/TaoAn03. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) and related nuclear transients probe jet launching, disk formation and circularization, particle acceleration, and the circumnuclear medium (CNM). However, the small fraction of events launching relativistic jets, the weak or delayed radio emission of many thermal TDEs, and the black-hole demographics of galactic nuclei remain poorly understood. SKA, with microJy sensitivity, wide bandwidth, long baselines, rapid response, and commensal surveys across 50-350 MHz (SKA-Low) and 0.35-15.4 GHz (SKA-Mid), will transform this field. Its sensitivity, frequency coverage, and very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) capability will extend radio calorimetry from a few well-studied nearby events to volume-limited samples of non-relativistic outflows. The SKA will bring off-axis and mildly relativistic jets into routine reach, trace CNM density profiles through the evolution of the low-frequency synchrotron turnover, and localize faint off-nuclear transients with sub-arcsecond precision. These data will constrain jet incidence, energetics, geometry, and magnetization, map the CNM through shock interactions, test links to changing-look active galactic nuclei (AGN) and high-energy neutrinos, and identify off-nuclear events associated with recoiling supermassive or intermediate-mass black holes. We discuss the benefits of commensal surveys, rapid triggering, and SKA-VLBI, and provide predictions based on the projected performance of AA* and AA4. SKA will shift TDE radio studies from detailed case-by-case studies to population-scale inference, advancing studies of jet physics and black-hole demographics.

title: Thermal Breaking of the I-Love Universality for Hot White Dwarfs
summary: The universal I-Love-Q relations for compact stars have significant applications in gravitational-wave astronomy, but thermal effects can break these relations in low-mass white dwarfs. In this work, we employ the stellar evolution code MESA to construct realistic models of $0.15 \, M_{\odot}$ helium-core and $0.6 \, M_{\odot}$ carbon-oxygen core white dwarfs at various temperatures. By utilizing the Clairaut-Radau equation, we quantitatively extract the radial variation of the eccentricity of internal isodensity surfaces. Our numerical results demonstrate that higher central temperatures amplify the eccentricity variation, causing the I-Love relations to deviate from the zero-temperature Chandrasekhar model, whereas subsequent cooling restores them. This confirms that the temperature-induced violation of the universal relations is fundamentally driven by the loss of self-similarity in isodensity surfaces, providing key insights into the applicability conditions of I-Love-Q relations in compact objects.

The violation is driven by loss of self-similarity in isodensity surfaces.

title: Impact of Kaon Condensation on the Thermal Evolution of the CCO in HESS J1731--347 Supernova Remnant
summary: Recent analyses of the central compact object in the HESS J1731--347 supernova remnant suggest an unusual combination of a low mass and small radius, while its thermal emission indicates a relatively high surface temperature at its estimated age. Reconciling these structural and thermal properties within a unified theoretical framework may provide important constraints on the equation of state and composition of dense matter. In this work, we investigate the thermal consequences of negatively charged kaon condensation, an exotic phase that softens the equation of state and facilitate the reproduction of the inferred bulk properties of HESS J1731--347. We find that the onset of kaon condensation strongly accelerates the thermal evolution, leading to surface temperature substantially below the observationally inferred range. Within the adopted cooling framework, kaon condensation therefore cannot simultaneously account for the structural and thermal properties of HESS J1731--347.

Reconciling these properties may constrain the equation of state and composition of dense matter, motivating a test of whether kaon condensation—which softens the EoS and can reproduce the inferred bulk properties—can also account for the thermal observations.

They then compute the thermal evolution of these configurations within the adopted cooling framework to compare predicted surface temperatures against observational constraints.

title: High-mass binary black hole mergers from detailed binary evolution models
summary:
Gravitational-wave observations reveal a population of binary black hole (BBH) mergers with primary masses above ${\sim}40\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, extending into and potentially beyond the pair-instability mass gap, with a possibly flat mass-ratio and broader χ_\mathrm{eff} distribution. We investigate whether super-Eddington accretion during stable mass transfer in isolated binary evolution can produce BBH mergers consistent with these properties across primary BH mass, mass-ratio, and χ_\mathrm{eff} distributions. Using POSYDON, we simulate BBH merger populations with primary BH masses above ${\sim}40\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, under three BH accretion efficiencies: Eddington-limited, GRRMHD-informed, and fully conservative. We additionally vary the natal kick strength, including strong kicks at high BH masses.
  We find that super-Eddington accretion does not suppress BBH mergers in the high-mass regime. Fully-conservative accretion leads to an increase of BBH mergers in POSYDON with a strong kick-independent peak at $χ_\mathrm{eff}=0.6$ and a sharp mass-ratio peak at $q\sim0.5$, whereas observations favor $χ_\mathrm{eff}=0.0$ and a flatter mass-ratio distribution. The GRRMHD-informed and Eddington-limited accretion are compatible with the observed primary BH mass and mass ratio distribution, but require natal kicks to populate negative χ_\mathrm{eff}.
  A joint analysis of the primary BH mass, mass ratio, and χ_\mathrm{eff} distributions provides strong constraints on binary evolution physics, and disfavor fully-conservative BH accretion as the dominant formation mechanism for high-mass BBH mergers. The Eddington-limited and GRRMHD-informed prescriptions with modest kicks can explain part of the high-mass population, but an additional formation channel is still needed to account for the high fraction of negative χ_\mathrm{eff} systems and high secondary BH spins.

title: Comparative Periodogram Analysis of 22 Years of Super-Kamiokande Solar $^{8}\mathrm{B}$ Neutrino Data: Classical, Phase-Based, and Information Theoretic Methods
summary: Solar $^8\mathrm{B}$ neutrinos offer a unique probe of solar interior dynamics and neutrino electromagnetic properties. We present a systematic, multi-method periodogram analysis of the 22-year Super-Kamiokande solar neutrino dataset (1996--2018), comparing nine algorithms. Through hierarchical temporal segmentation, we disentangle astrophysical signals from detector systematics. The Generalized Lomb-Scargle (GLS) method provides the most statistically robust detections by correctly handling heteroscedastic uncertainties, whereas classical Lomb-Scargle systematically underestimates significance. The Lafler--Kinman method generally fails, whereas independent algorithms like MHAOV and PDM1 recover consistent periodicities, providing vital cross-validation. In pre-2001 and SK-I data, seven algorithms provide \textit{weak evidence} ($\ln B > 0$) for a $\sim 38.8$ d periodicity. However, this signal is entirely absent in the highest-statistics SK-IV modified flux data, where the Bayes factor decisively favors the null model ($\ln B \ll -5$), indicating it is a transient feature of the early low-statistics era. Conversely, a $\sim 24.3$ d signal in post-2001 raw flux is decisively rejected by the Bayesian framework and vanishes in modified flux, confirming its seasonal systematic origin. Furthermore, no evidence is found for an $\sim 11$-year solar cycle modulation, yielding a stringent amplitude upper limit of $<0.2\%$ of the mean flux. By highlighting the stark contrast between frequentist significance and Bayesian model selection ($\ln B$) in low signal-to-noise regimes, we establish a rigorous, multi-metric best-practice framework for periodicity searches. This work provides a direct methodological blueprint for next-generation observatories like Hyper-Kamiokande and JUNO.

title: The First Measurement of Jet Collimation Profiles in an X-ray Binary: the Case of SS 433
comment: This is a revised manuscript submitted to ApJL
summary: While significant progress has been achieved in active galactic nuclei (AGN), jet collimation profiles in X-ray binaries (XRBs) have not been directly measured. Here we report the first measurement of jet collimation profiles in an XRB using very long baseline interferometry data from SS 433. The approaching jet exhibits a well-constrained quasi-parabolic profile in the 1995 and 1998 data, whereas the prominent local oscillations present in the 2000 jet-width measurements preclude a robust characterization of the jet collimation profile. Nevertheless, the 2000 data suggest that the intrinsic jet opening angle decreases gradually from $\sim 20^\circ$ at 8$\times 10^{14}$ cm to $\sim 3^\circ$ at $9\times 10^{15}$ cm (deprojected), providing evidence for progressive jet collimation. The width and opening angle of the receding jet are also presented, although their interpretation is limited by the free--free absorption effect. In addition, we measure the frequency-dependent core positions at four bands and derive a core-shift relation. These results establish SS 433 as the first XRB in which jet collimation, opening-angle evolution, and core-shift relation are constrained.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first direct measurement of jet collimation profiles in an X-ray binary (XRB) using VLBI observations of SS 433. The approaching jet shows a quasi-parabolic profile in 1995/1998 data, while 2000 data, though affected by oscillations, indicate a gradual decrease in intrinsic opening angle from ~20° to ~3° over a deprojected distance range, providing evidence for progressive jet collimation. The authors also measure frequency-dependent core positions and derive a core-shift relation, establishing SS 433 as the first XRB with constrained jet collimation, opening-angle evolution, and core-shift.
AI.motivation: While jet collimation profiles have been extensively studied in active galactic nuclei (AGN), they had never been directly measured in X-ray binaries (XRBs). This work aims to fill that gap by measuring jet collimation profiles in an XRB for the first time.
AI.method: The authors used very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) data from the XRB SS 433 across multiple epochs (1995, 1998, 2000) to measure jet width as a function of distance. They characterized the jet collimation profile (e.g., quasi-parabolic vs. oscillatory), measured intrinsic opening angles, examined the receding jet accounting for free-free absorption, and used multi-frequency observations to measure core positions and derive the core-shift relation.
AI.result: The approaching jet exhibits a well-constrained quasi-parabolic collimation profile in 1995 and 1998. The 2000 data show local oscillations that prevent robust characterization, but suggest the intrinsic opening angle decreases from ~20° at 8×10^14 cm to ~3° at 9×10^15 cm (deprojected), confirming progressive collimation. Receding jet widths and opening angles were also measured, limited by free-free absorption. Frequency-dependent core positions at four bands enabled a core-shift relation to be derived.
AI.conclusion: SS 433 is established as the first XRB in which jet collimation, opening-angle evolution, and core-shift relation have all been constrained, providing a new observational benchmark for comparing jet physics between XRBs and AGN.

title: Multiwavelength study of supernova remnants in the Circinus constellation with SRG/eROSITA
summary: Supernova remnants (SNRs) are key tracers of stellar feedback and the chemical and dynamical evolution of the interstellar medium. However, identifying SNRs in complex regions remains challenging, particularly when only archival multi-wavelength data are available. We aim to search for previously unrecognized SNR candidates in the Circinus constellation by combining optical imaging, radio continuum data, and available SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey X-ray observations, to provide a prioritized list of targets for future confirmation. Candidate remnants were classified according to the strength of the combined diagnostics. This joint analysis yields improved constraints on the morphology and spectral properties of known remnants in the region, including MSH 15-52 and G320.6- 1.6. In addition, we identify a new promising SNR candidate, G320.2-3.6. Our study provides a first multi-wavelength search of SNR candidates in the Circinus region. In addition to G320.2-3.6, three objects (G319.8-2.0, G321.8-1.1, and G320.5-1.8) emerge as promising targets for follow-up radio, spectroscopic optical, and deeper, spatially resolved X-ray observations to confirm their nature.

AI.tldr: A multi-wavelength search for supernova remnant (SNR) candidates in the Circinus constellation, combining optical, radio, and SRG/eROSITA X-ray data. The study refines the morphology and spectral properties of known remnants (MSH 15-52, G320.6-1.6) and identifies a new promising candidate, G320.2-3.6, plus three additional follow-up targets.
AI.motivation: SNRs are key tracers of stellar feedback and chemical/dynamical evolution of the interstellar medium, but identifying them in complex regions using only archival multi-wavelength data is challenging.
AI.method: Combined analysis of optical imaging, radio continuum data, and SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey X-ray observations; candidates were classified according to the strength of combined diagnostics.
AI.result: Improved constraints on known remnants (MSH 15-52, G320.6-1.6); identification of a new promising SNR candidate G320.2-3.6, and three additional follow-up targets (G319.8-2.0, G321.8-1.1, G320.5-1.8).
AI.conclusion: This is the first multi-wavelength search of SNR candidates in the Circinus region, providing a prioritized list of targets for future radio, spectroscopic optical, and deeper X-ray confirmation observations.

title: Estimating amplitude of matter density fluctuations in solar and supernova models using neutrino flavor evolution
summary: Neutrinos can undergo substantial flavor evolution between their production in astrophysical sources-such as the Sun and core-collapse supernovae-and their subsequent detection in terrestrial detectors. This flavor evolution is strongly influenced by the environment that the neutrinos interact with, making them useful astrophysical messengers capable of potentially carrying information about the properties of the source wherein they are produced. In this work, we apply the framework of statistical data assimilation (SDA) in order to ascertain the extent to which a neutrino signal at detection may contain information about matter density fluctuations along their path from the source. Using simplified models of neutrino flavor evolution and propagation in the sun and in a core-collapse supernova (CCSN), we find that the SDA method is able to extract information about the amplitude of density fluctuations in both the solar and CCSN scenarios, with the method showing relatively greater reliability in the solar neutrino case. Nonetheless, even in the CCSN neutrino model, the method proved effective at high fluctuation amplitudes

AI.tldr: This paper applies statistical data assimilation (SDA) to determine whether neutrino flavor signals detected on Earth can reveal information about matter density fluctuations along their propagation path from astrophysical sources. Using simplified solar and core-collapse supernova (CCSN) neutrino evolution models, the SDA method successfully extracts density fluctuation amplitudes in both scenarios, with higher reliability for solar neutrinos, though still effective for CCSN neutrinos at high fluctuation amplitudes.
AI.motivation: Neutrino flavor evolution is strongly influenced by their surrounding environment, making neutrinos potentially valuable astrophysical messengers capable of carrying information about source properties. The authors aim to ascertain whether detectable neutrino signals can reveal information about matter density fluctuations along their propagation path.
AI.method: The authors apply the statistical data assimilation (SDA) framework to simplified models of neutrino flavor evolution and propagation in two astrophysical contexts: the Sun and a core-collapse supernova.
AI.result: The SDA method successfully extracts information about the amplitude of density fluctuations in both solar and CCSN scenarios. The method demonstrates relatively greater reliability in the solar neutrino case, while remaining effective for CCSN neutrinos at high fluctuation amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: Statistical data assimilation is a viable tool for extracting information about matter density fluctuations from neutrino flavor signals, showing promise as a technique for probing astrophysical source environments, particularly in the solar case and for high-amplitude fluctuations in CCSN scenarios.

title: Binary neutron stars in the next-generation era: Multi-messenger detection prospects and constraints on the equation of state, mass distribution, and cosmology
summary: Next-generation gravitational-wave (GW) observatories will provide crucial insights into the nature of neutron star (NS) matter and the cosmological expansion history. We estimate the number of multi-messenger detections from binary neutron stars (BNS) with the Einstein Telescope (ET) and Cosmic Explorer (CE), and project the resulting constraints on the equation of state (EOS), BNS mass distribution, and cosmology via joint hierarchical Bayesian inference. Assuming a local merger rate of 106.6 Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$ and considering two different mass functions, a narrow one centred around 1.4 $M_\odot$ and a wide one ranging between 1.1--2 $M_\odot$, we find that for ET, our mock follow-up algorithm results in at least $\sim40$ and up to $\sim100$ successfully identified electromagnetic counterparts per year, depending on the detector layout and mass distribution. In a joint network with CE, the number of multi-messenger detections can range from $\sim 200$ to $\sim500$. Additionally, several more afterglows from gamma-ray bursts or KNe could be found with dedicated late-time observations. Based on the identified multi-messenger events, we perform an injection campaign to hierarchically constrain the EOS, mass distribution, and cosmology in a fully Bayesian framework. Focussing on ET alone, we show how in an ideal scenario, GW signals, KNe, and host galaxy redshifts can constrain the canonical NS radius $R_{1.4}$ within $\sim 0.2$ km and the Hubble constant $H_0$ within $\sim 1$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, while recovering the essential features of the mass distribution. By comparing inference results that rely solely on GW data and those that incorporate light curve information, we find that while KN light-curve posteriors have a negligible impact on the EOS constraints, they can benefit the inference of cosmological parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper estimates the number of multi-messenger detections from binary neutron star mergers with the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, and projects resulting constraints on the neutron star equation of state, BNS mass distribution, and cosmology via hierarchical Bayesian inference. With ET alone, 40-100 electromagnetic counterparts per year are expected, and 200-500 with the ET+CE network. These events can constrain R1.4 to ~0.2 km and H0 to ~1 km/s/Mpc, with KN light-curve data benefiting cosmological but not EOS constraints.
AI.motivation: Next-generation GW observatories will provide crucial insights into neutron star matter and the cosmological expansion history. The authors aim to quantify the scientific potential of multi-messenger BNS observations with ET and CE, and project the constraining power on EOS, mass distribution, and cosmology.
AI.method: The authors simulate BNS merger populations using a local merger rate of 106.6 Gpc^-3 yr^-1, considering narrow (around 1.4 M_sun) and wide (1.1-2 M_sun) mass distributions. They use a mock follow-up algorithm to estimate electromagnetic counterpart identification rates for ET and ET+CE networks. They perform an injection campaign with fully Bayesian hierarchical inference to jointly constrain the EOS, mass distribution, and cosmology using GW signals, kilonova light curves, and host galaxy redshifts.
AI.result: For ET, at least ~40 and up to ~100 successfully identified EM counterparts per year are found; with the ET+CE network this ranges from ~200 to ~500. In ideal scenarios, R1.4 can be constrained to ~0.2 km and H0 to ~1 km/s/Mpc. KN light-curve posteriors have negligible impact on EOS constraints but benefit cosmological parameter inference.
AI.conclusion: Next-generation GW observatories will enable a rich multi-messenger BNS detection program, providing high-precision constraints on the EOS and cosmology. Kilonova light curves primarily help cosmological inference rather than EOS constraints, informing observational strategy priorities.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Tidal Disruption Event Classification : A Host-Agnostic Probabilistic Random Forest Approach
summary: The classification of Tidal Disruption Events in large-scale photometric surveys is challenging because deterministic machine learning models produce overconfident misclassifications under varying data quality and low signal-to-noise conditions. Existing lightcurve-based approaches fail to incorporate measurement uncertainties, consequently generating brittle outputs. We present a host-agnostic, uncertainty-aware classification framework using a Probabilistic Random Forest (PRF). Our pipeline extracts 11 characteristic features from nuclear transients in the ZTF alert stream, including rise and decay timescales, blackbody temperature evolution, and pre-transient variability metrics. Relying exclusively on photometric data without host galaxy information ensures effectiveness for the faint transient population expected from the Rubin Observatory. The PRF, which treats feature measurements as distributions, was evaluated against XGBoost through Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation. It yields higher stability and robustness for ambiguous candidates than XGBoost. The two classifiers occupy complementary regimes. XGBoost achieves higher recall in balanced and high-precision scenarios, where its rigid decision boundaries efficiently isolate TDE-like sources, while PRF rejects more false positives by penalizing sources with large feature uncertainties. Applying this framework to archival data identified 11 new candidate TDEs from the unclassified population and 3 potential photometric TDEs within existing training labels previously misclassified as supernovae or active galactic nuclei. This work demonstrates that TDEs can be reliably identified using photometric lightcurve features, providing a host-independent framework. Uncertainty-aware, probabilistic classifiers are essential for the Rubin era to prevent the overconfident misclassifications inherent in deterministic models at low signal-to-noise.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an uncertainty-aware classification framework using a Probabilistic Random Forest (PRF) to identify Tidal Disruption Events (TDEs) from ZTF photometric lightcurves. The host-agnostic pipeline extracts 11 features from nuclear transients and treats measurements as distributions, outperforming deterministic XGBoost in robustness and false-positive rejection. Applied to archival data, it identified 11 new TDE candidates and 3 previously misclassified sources.
AI.motivation: Deterministic machine learning models overconfidently misclassify TDEs in large-scale photometric surveys under varying data quality and low signal-to-noise conditions. Existing lightcurve-based approaches ignore measurement uncertainties, producing brittle outputs—a problem that will be exacerbated in the Rubin Observatory era.
AI.method: A Probabilistic Random Forest (PRF) is used to classify TDEs from 11 extracted lightcurve features (rise/decay timescales, blackbody temperature evolution, pre-transient variability) in ZTF alert stream data. The framework is host-agnostic, treating feature measurements as probability distributions to propagate uncertainties, and is evaluated against XGBoost via Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation.
AI.result: PRF shows higher stability and robustness for ambiguous candidates than XGBoost. The two classifiers occupy complementary regimes: XGBoost achieves higher recall in balanced and high-precision scenarios, while PRF rejects more false positives by penalizing uncertain features. Application to archival data found 11 new TDE candidates and 3 potential photometric TDEs previously misclassified as supernovae or AGN.
AI.conclusion: TDEs can be reliably identified using photometric lightcurve features alone without host galaxy information. Uncertainty-aware probabilistic classifiers are essential for the Rubin era to prevent overconfident misclassifications inherent in deterministic models at low signal-to-noise.

title: Same explosion, many faces: numerical modeling reveals viewing angle as a driver of diversity for core-collapse SNe in binary systems
comment: 19 pages, 12 figures, submitted to AAS journals. Comments are welcome
summary: Observable properties of core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) depend sensitively on the circumstellar material (CSM) formed by pre-explosion mass loss from the progenitor star. Since a large fraction of CCSN progenitors reside in binaries, both the progenitor structure and surrounding CSM can be significantly impacted by binary interaction. Yet, its impact on the observed CCSN landscape remains poorly constrained. In this work, we investigate CCSNe from binary systems undergoing stable Roche lobe overflow. We construct a suite of binary evolution models in \texttt{MESA} with a fixed initial primary mass ($16M_{\odot}$), exploring secondary masses in the range $12-15M_{\odot}$ and initial orbital periods $>500$ days. We generate three-dimensional (3D) CSM structures from the resulting mass-loss histories and orbital dynamics, extract angle-dependent density profiles along three lines of sight, and compute multi-band light curves with the radiation-hydrodynamics code \texttt{Stella}. We find that binary-driven CSM develops highly aspherical morphologies, governed by the orbital period and the mass ratio. Interaction between SN ejecta and this structured medium produces pronounced viewing-angle dependence in the light curves, with peak luminosities differing by factors of $\sim5$ and late-time $B-V$ colors varying by $\sim1.5$ mag depending on observer orientation. We further show that interpreting such events with one-dimensional frameworks assuming isolated progenitors and spherical winds can introduce biases up to $50\%$ for inferred explosion properties and $>200\%$ for inferred mass-loss rates. Our results are consistent with a substantial fraction of interacting Type II SN diversity arising from binary-shaped asymmetric CSM and viewing-angle effects, motivating multidimensional approaches to interpreting these transients.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) from binary systems undergoing stable Roche lobe overflow, constructing binary evolution models with MESA, generating 3D CSM structures, and computing multi-band light curves with Stella. The binary-driven CSM is highly aspherical, producing viewing-angle-dependent light curves with peak luminosities differing by factors of ~5 and B-V colors varying by ~1.5 mag. Using 1D frameworks assuming isolated progenitors can bias inferred explosion properties by up to 50% and mass-loss rates by >200%, suggesting a substantial fraction of interacting Type II SN diversity arises from binary-shaped asymmetric CSM and viewing-angle effects.
AI.motivation: A large fraction of CCSN progenitors reside in binaries, and binary interaction significantly impacts both progenitor structure and surrounding CSM, yet its effect on the observed CCSN landscape remains poorly constrained. Understanding how binary-driven asymmetric CSM shapes supernova light curves is crucial for correctly interpreting observations.
AI.method: The authors construct binary evolution models in MESA with a fixed initial primary mass of 16 solar masses, exploring secondary masses of 12-15 solar masses and initial orbital periods >500 days for systems undergoing stable Roche lobe overflow. They generate 3D CSM structures from mass-loss histories and orbital dynamics, extract angle-dependent density profiles along three lines of sight, and compute multi-band light curves using the radiation-hydrodynamics code Stella.
AI.result: Binary-driven CSM develops highly aspherical morphologies governed by orbital period and mass ratio. SN ejecta interaction with this structured medium produces pronounced viewing-angle dependence: peak luminosities differ by factors of ~5 and late-time B-V colors vary by ~1.5 mag depending on observer orientation. Interpreting such events with 1D frameworks (assuming isolated progenitors and spherical winds) introduces biases up to 50% for inferred explosion properties and >200% for inferred mass-loss rates.
AI.conclusion: A substantial fraction of interacting Type II SN diversity is likely attributable to binary-shaped asymmetric CSM and viewing-angle effects. This motivates multidimensional approaches to interpreting these transients rather than relying on spherically symmetric 1D models.

title: Search for gravitational waves associated with high-energy neutrinos detected by IceCube during the third observing run of LIGO-Virgo
summary: We search for generic gravitational-wave transients associated with high-energy neutrinos detected by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory during the third Observing Run (O3) of Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA. We perform an unmodeled, targeted search, which is sensitive to gravitational-wave signals weaker than those reported in real time or in the gravitional-wave transient catalog, and can thus uncover coincidences missed by typical neutrino follow-up searches. We find no statistically significant gravitational-wave signal and set lower bounds on the distance of possible gravitational-wave sources for different emission models.

AI.tldr: A targeted, unmodeled search for gravitational-wave transients coincident with IceCube high-energy neutrinos during LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA's third observing run finds no statistically significant signal, and sets lower distance bounds on possible gravitational-wave sources under various emission models.
AI.motivation: To uncover gravitational-wave signals coincident with high-energy neutrinos that may be missed by real-time or catalog-based follow-ups, since such multi-messenger coincidences could reveal hidden astrophysical sources.
AI.method: An unmodeled, targeted search for generic gravitational-wave transients at times and sky positions of IceCube-detected high-energy neutrinos during O3, sensitive to signals weaker than those reported in real time or in the transient catalog.
AI.result: No statistically significant gravitational-wave signal was found, and lower bounds on the distances of potential sources were established for different emission models.
AI.conclusion: The search sets improved distance constraints on potential gravitational-wave sources associated with high-energy neutrinos, but finds no evidence for such coincident multi-messenger events in O3.

title: Spinning down neutron-star merger remnants with the Tayler-Spruit dynamo: Global simulations reveal the formation of massive disks and neutron-rich ejecta
summary: Magnetic-field amplification and angular momentum (AM) transport critically shape the secular evolution, lifetime, and electromagnetic signatures of binary neutron-star merger remnants. While the magnetorotational instability can operate in the outer negative-shear regions of the neutron-star remnant and accretion disk, the positive-shear, stably stratified core may instead be susceptible to the Tayler-Spruit dynamo. We present the first global, long-term general-relativistic neutrino-radiation magnetohydrodynamics simulations of a neutron-star merger remnant incorporating the unresolved Tayler-Spruit dynamo through a new mean-field dynamo subgrid prescription. Our axisymmetric simulations starting from a realistic merger remnant show that the Tayler-Spruit dynamo is primarily active in high-latitude regions of the remnant core. The resulting Maxwell stresses redistribute AM on a spin-down timescale of a few hundred milliseconds, substantially flattening the core rotation profile and transferring mass and AM from the outer remnant into the disk. This produces a more massive, extended, and strongly magnetized disk with a low electron fraction, leading to substantially more neutron-rich ejecta. Our results demonstrate that currently unmodelled Tayler-Spruit dynamo action can qualitatively alter the rotational evolution, collapse prospects, disk formation, and multi-messenger signatures of long-lived neutron-star merger remnants.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first global, long-term general-relativistic neutrino-radiation MHD simulations of a neutron-star merger remnant that incorporate the unresolved Tayler-Spruit dynamo via a new mean-field dynamo subgrid prescription. The simulations show the dynamo is active mainly in high-latitude core regions, redistributing angular momentum on a few hundred millisecond timescale, flattening the core rotation profile, and producing a more massive, extended, strongly magnetized, neutron-rich disk with enhanced ejecta. This demonstrates that the Tayler-Spruit dynamo can qualitatively change the rotational evolution, collapse prospects, disk formation, and multi-messenger signatures of long-lived merger remnants.
AI.motivation: Magnetic-field amplification and angular momentum transport (via the magnetorotational instability in outer regions and potentially the Tayler-Spruit dynamo in the positive-shear, stably stratified core) critically shape the evolution and electromagnetic signatures of binary neutron-star merger remnants, but the Tayler-Spruit dynamo had not been incorporated into global simulations.
AI.method: Global, axisymmetric, long-term general-relativistic neutrino-radiation magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations starting from a realistic merger remnant, with the unresolved Tayler-Spruit dynamo modeled through a newly developed mean-field dynamo subgrid prescription.
AI.result: The Tayler-Spruit dynamo is primarily active in high-latitude regions of the remnant core, generating Maxwell stresses that spin down the core on a ~few hundred millisecond timescale, flattening the rotation profile, and transferring mass/angular momentum into the disk. This yields a more massive, extended, strongly magnetized disk with low electron fraction and substantially more neutron-rich ejecta.
AI.conclusion: The Tayler-Spruit dynamo, previously unmodeled in such simulations, can qualitatively alter the rotational evolution, collapse prospects, disk formation, and multi-messenger signatures of long-lived neutron-star merger remnants.

title: A Four-dimensional Model-agnostic Probe into the Astrophysical Origins of Binary Black Hole Subpopulations
summary: There is strong evidence of multiple binary black hole~(BBH) subpopulations in the cumulative gravitational wave catalog by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration that likely originate through distinct evolutionary channels. The astrophysical interpretation of this complex underlying population is subject to theoretical uncertainties in treatments of binary stellar evolution, core collapse, and host environments. Due to a lack of robust predictions and the sheer diversity of plausible features, strongly modelled population analyses often lead to prior-driven conclusions. On the other hand, flexible alternatives are often difficult to scale in higher dimensions, which can lead to a loss of critical information on astrophysically meaningful correlations. In this \textit{Letter}, we present the first data-driven reconstruction of the joint four-dimensional distribution of BBH primary masses, mass ratios, effective inspiral and effective precessing spin parameters, which yields novel model-agnostic constraints on the astrophysical origins of BBH subpopulations. We characterize four distinct subpopulations spanning different ranges of BBH masses and report new correlations in these specific mass ranges that are beyond the reach of strongly modeled parametrizations and lower-dimensional data-driven frameworks. Our results unveil novel insights into the abundances of specific subchannels of isolated binary evolution, dynamical assembly, and hierarchical mergers across various mass ranges in the astrophysical BBH population.

AI.tldr: This letter presents the first data-driven reconstruction of the joint four-dimensional distribution of binary black hole primary masses, mass ratios, effective inspiral spin, and effective precessing spin parameters, revealing four distinct subpopulations and new mass-dependent correlations that inform on isolated binary evolution, dynamical assembly, and hierarchical mergers.
AI.motivation: Existing BBH population analyses face a fundamental trade-off: strongly modeled approaches are prior-driven and unreliable due to theoretical uncertainties in stellar evolution and core collapse, while flexible alternatives struggle to scale to higher dimensions and lose critical astrophysical correlations. A model-agnostic, high-dimensional approach is needed to robustly characterize the complex underlying BBH population.
AI.method: The authors perform a data-driven (model-agnostic) reconstruction of the joint four-dimensional distribution of BBH primary masses, mass ratios, effective inspiral spin, and effective precessing spin using gravitational wave data from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA catalogs, enabling recovery of multidimensional correlations without assuming specific parametric models.
AI.result: The analysis identifies four distinct BBH subpopulations spanning different mass ranges and reveals novel correlations within these mass ranges that were previously inaccessible to strongly parametrized models or lower-dimensional data-driven frameworks. These results provide new model-agnostic constraints on the abundances of subchannels from isolated binary evolution, dynamical assembly, and hierarchical mergers.
AI.conclusion: The data-driven approach overcomes the limitations of both strongly modeled and simplistic flexible frameworks, delivering novel astrophysical insights into the origins of BBH subpopulations and highlighting subchannel abundances across various mass ranges that were previously unconstrained.
